Producer products do not exclude equipment leasing for being non-physical. Businesses buy leased access as an operating input, which keeps those contracts inside the producer-product service set.

“Physical components only” would erase leasing, maintenance, and software from producer products — not the chapter’s rule.

If that ban were real, shipping lines could never book leased gear as a producer-product purchase; they can and do.

Carriers booking leased gear buy operating capacity — producer-product service — so physical-components-only cannot stand.

So the statement is False.

Marketing includes chemical solvent among products when it is exchanged to fulfil the production needs of a logistics company. Exchange plus manufacturing or processing need is the producer-product goods path.

So the statement is True.

DIY solvent sold to a resident still enters marketing’s product set as a consumer good. The household purchase is exchange that meets a personal project wish, which is enough for the consumer-product reading.

Look at the hardware aisle: small can, resident, weekend repair — consumer-product goods trade beside the bulk B2B drums of the same chemistry.

Both the drum and the can enter the product set once each is exchanged to meet its own buyer’s wishes.

So the statement is True.

title: Marketing Objectives Overview
context: Analyze how businesses set marketing objectives after analysing the markets they wish to operate in. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: If customers are not satisfied with the product, they are unlikely to buy it again.
Satisfied customers often become loyal customers who may purchase the product again.
Customer satisfaction is unrelated to whether buyers purchase the product again.
Customer satisfaction as a marketing objective is interrelated with objectives such as sales and loyalty.
Meeting customer wishes and needs is a prerequisite for defining meaningful marketing objectives.
tactical_explanations:
If customers are not satisfied with the product, they are unlikely to buy it again — that link is why satisfaction sits among marketing objectives rather than as a soft side note.

A sportswear buyer who finds seams splitting after one wash rarely returns for the next colourway. Lost repeats show up later as thinner sales, so firms treat contentment as something to pursue on purpose.

Satisfaction objectives sit beside sales targets because the second purchase is where contentment proves commercial worth.

So the statement is True.

Satisfied buyers often turn into loyal customers who may purchase again. Contentment after use is the bridge from a one-off trial to a returning household or athlete.

Loyalty programmes amplify that bridge; they do not invent it from thin air when the product disappointed.

So the statement is True.

Customer satisfaction is tightly related to repurchase, not unrelated. Buyers who leave disappointed rarely return on loyalty alone, and firms that shrug “satisfaction doesn’t matter for next purchase” fight the chapter’s objective map.

Picture a dairy brand that wins a trial with a coupon but ships flat-tasting milk: the next shop visit goes to a rival even if the logo was memorable. Satisfaction and repurchase travel together in the framework.

If that link were optional, marketing could chase ads forever without caring whether the product landed — which is not how these objectives are taught.

So the statement is False.

Customer satisfaction as a marketing objective is interrelated with objectives such as sales and loyalty. Meeting wishes supports repeats; repeats support volume; volume feeds the commercial scoreboard.

Treating satisfaction as a sealed-off soft goal misses those cross-links the chapter stresses.

So the statement is True.

Meeting customer wishes and needs is a prerequisite for defining meaningful marketing objectives. Without that analysis, targets for sales, share, or loyalty float free of what buyers actually want.

So the statement is True.

title: Customer Satisfaction and Loyalty
context: Consider a sportswear manufacturer investing in distinctive product design, athlete endorsements, and loyalty programmes to stand apart from rivals. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A business that ignores customer satisfaction risks losing repeat sales from otherwise viable buyers.
A dissatisfied customer may still become a loyal repeat buyer without any change in the product.
Post-purchase satisfaction influences whether a customer considers the product for a future purchase.
Customer satisfaction is the only marketing objective and replaces sales and profit goals.
Businesses set marketing objectives without analysing customer wishes and needs.
tactical_explanations:
A business that ignores customer satisfaction risks losing repeat sales from otherwise viable buyers who simply will not come back after a poor experience.

Viable demand still walks away when the product fails them; ignoring satisfaction burns that second sale.

So the statement is True.

A dissatisfied customer does not become a loyal repeat buyer with no change in the product. Loyalty in this chapter grows from satisfactory experience, not from stubborn habit on top of disappointment.

Leaving the offer untouched while hoping for loyalty invents a shortcut the framework does not grant.

So the statement is False.

Post-purchase satisfaction influences whether a customer considers the product for a future purchase. The first-use experience is a memory that either opens the door to a second buy or closes it.

Sportswear that felt great in training earns a place on the next shopping list; gear that blistered feet does not. That after-use verdict is why firms measure satisfaction as an objective, not only as a smile metric.

: the sale is not finished at checkout — the use phase still votes on the next sale.

Checkout celebrations without post-use feedback leave managers blind on whether the next purchase will happen.

So the statement is True.

Customer satisfaction is one marketing objective among several; it does not replace sales and profit goals. The framework keeps those targets on the board together rather than crowning satisfaction as the only aim.

Firms still need volume and margin; satisfaction supports them instead of deleting them.

So the statement is False.

Businesses set marketing objectives after analysing customer wishes and needs, not without that work. Skipping needs analysis leaves objectives unanchored — sales targets without a sense of what would satisfy buyers.

A strong logo does not excuse empty listening. The chapter puts wishes-and-needs work before meaningful objective setting.

So the statement is False.

title: Unique Selling Proposition Basics
context: Analyze how a unique selling proposition supports product differentiation and attracts loyal customers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Loyal customers who buy again help sustain sales volume over time.
Customer satisfaction supports retention rather than relying solely on one-off transactions.
Satisfied customers rarely buy the product again because loyalty is independent of satisfaction.
Satisfied customers may recommend the product to others, extending marketing impact beyond the original sale.
Customer satisfaction objectives apply only to service firms, not to goods producers.
tactical_explanations:
Loyal customers who buy again help sustain sales volume over time, turning satisfaction into recurring revenue rather than a string of one-off hunts for new trialists.

Retention keeps the volume line from resetting to zero every period.

So the statement is True.

Satisfaction supports retention instead of relying only on one-off transactions. A firm that only counts first purchases while ignoring whether buyers were content builds a leaky bucket.

Retention objectives and satisfaction objectives lean on each other in the chapter’s map.

So the statement is True.

Satisfied customers are more likely to buy again; loyalty is not independent of satisfaction. The claim reverses the chapter: it treats loyalty as floating free while satisfied buyers “rarely” return — which fights everyday repurchase logic.

Walk a coffee habit: the cup that tasted right yesterday is why the same customer returns tomorrow. Satisfaction feeds that loop; it does not block it.

Loyalty schemes that ignore whether the cup tasted right build on sand; satisfaction is the load-bearing piece.

So the statement is False.

Satisfied customers may recommend the product to others, extending marketing impact beyond the original sale. Word of mouth multiplies a good experience into new trial without another full acquisition spend.

That spillover is one reason satisfaction belongs on the objective list, not only repurchase.

So the statement is True.

Customer satisfaction objectives apply to goods producers as well as service firms. Tangible products still must meet wishes; a disappointing shoe loses repeats just as a cold hotel room does.

Limiting satisfaction goals to services invents a sector ban the framework does not carry. Goods brands measure contentment because physical use can fail buyers too.

Disappointing trainers lose athletes the way cold rooms lose guests — goods producers stay inside satisfaction objectives.

Note: goods versus services changes delivery form, not whether satisfaction matters as an objective.

So the statement is False.

title: Market Share as Competitiveness
context: Review why gaining and maintaining market share indicates a firm's relative competitiveness. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Repeat purchase behaviour proves that customer satisfaction objectives are unnecessary.
Marketing objectives include ensuring customers are content enough to consider repurchasing.
Dissatisfied customers are a signal that marketing and product delivery may be missing stated objectives.
Marketing objectives exclude customer satisfaction when profitability is prioritised.
Dissatisfied customers will still buy again if the price is reduced slightly.
tactical_explanations:
Repeat purchases do not prove that customer satisfaction objectives are unnecessary. Repeats can coexist with active satisfaction work; they are often the result of that work, not a licence to drop it.

Seeing loyalty today and declaring satisfaction “optional” misreads the cause.

So the statement is False.

Marketing objectives include ensuring customers are content enough to consider repurchasing. Satisfaction sits on the objective board because contentment is what makes the next purchase plausible.

Firms that only chase first-time volume while ignoring post-use feelings fight that design.

So the statement is True.

Dissatisfied customers signal that marketing and product delivery may be missing stated objectives. Rising complaints or falling scores are early warnings that sales and loyalty goals are at risk.

Treating discontent as noise rather than a signal wastes the feedback the chapter expects managers to use.

So the statement is True.

Marketing objectives do not drop customer satisfaction merely because profitability is prioritised. Profit and satisfaction are interrelated: content buyers support the repeat revenue that helps profit.

Prioritising margin is not a veto on listening. The framework keeps both on the map rather than forcing an either-or.

If profit priority erased satisfaction, firms could chase margin while burning the customer base — the opposite of the long-run story taught here.

Dairy co-ops chasing margin still survey taste because profit without returning households is a short season.

So the statement is False.

A slight price cut does not reliably make dissatisfied customers buy again. Discontent with the product experience outruns a small discount when the core offer still disappoints.

Picture a bakery that burns the loaf then knocks five percent off: the next weekend shopper still remembers the charcoal taste. Price can help trial; it does not cancel a failed experience.

A bakery that burns the loaf then knocks five percent off rarely resurrects loyalty while the charcoal memory remains.

So the statement is False.

title: Sales Volume and Revenue
context: Consider a dairy cooperative that brands its organic milk line, measures shelf share in supermarkets, and reinvests surplus profit into processing equipment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Customer satisfaction is measured only after profitability targets have been met.
Customer satisfaction surveys can inform how well a business is meeting its marketing objectives.
A firm pursuing loyalty must first address whether customers are satisfied with the core product.
Loyal customers emerge without any need for prior satisfaction with the product.
Repeat purchase behaviour is more likely when prior use met or exceeded customer expectations.
tactical_explanations:
Satisfaction is not postponed until after profitability targets are already met. Firms work satisfaction alongside commercial targets rather than treating it as a luxury phase after profit is banked.

Waiting for perfect profit before listening leaves the customer base unprotected during the wait.

Waiting for perfect profit before listening leaves the organic-milk base unprotected during the wait.

So the statement is False.

Customer satisfaction surveys can inform how well a business is meeting its marketing objectives by revealing whether buyers feel wishes were fulfilled. Scores and comments are evidence for objective reviews, not decoration.

So the statement is True.

A firm pursuing loyalty must first address whether customers are satisfied with the core product. Loyalty programmes layered on a disappointing offer reward people for staying with something they dislike — which rarely builds true loyalty.

Dairy co-ops that brand organic milk still need the milk to taste right; points cards cannot replace that core contentment.

: loyalty is an amplifier of satisfaction, not a substitute for it.

Stamp cards on sour milk do not create loyalty; they advertise that the firm misunderstood the sequence.

So the statement is True.

Loyal customers do not emerge without prior satisfaction with the product. Rewards schemes cannot invent loyalty on top of a failed experience; the chapter ties loyalty outcomes to satisfactory prior use.

Skipping satisfaction while hunting “loyal” badges reverses the sequence.

So the statement is False.

Repeat purchase behaviour is more likely when prior use met or exceeded customer expectations. That expectation match is why satisfaction work supports the repurchase objective rather than floating beside it.

Met expectations open the door to the next buy; missed ones close it.

So the statement is True.

title: Profitability Objective Foundations
context: Review profitability as a marketing objective and its link to reimbursing owners and reinvestment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Customer satisfaction has no connection to market share or sales volume objectives.
A business can ignore wishes and needs analysis if it already has a strong brand.
Customer satisfaction is not separable from long-run sales performance in the marketing framework.
Satisfaction objectives mean customers must be delighted on every dimension or they will never return.
Customer complaints rising after a campaign indicate success on satisfaction objectives.
tactical_explanations:
Satisfaction connects to market share and sales volume; it is not an isolated soft metric with no commercial link. Content buyers return and recommend; that behaviour feeds share and sales objectives.

So the statement is False.

A strong brand does not excuse skipping wishes-and-needs analysis. Brands still need products that match what buyers want; reputation without listening eventually hollows out.

Famous logos still need products that match wishes; skipping needs work because the brand feels strong is how brands hollow out.

So the statement is False.

Customer satisfaction is not separable from long-run sales performance in the marketing framework. Content buyers return, complain less, and keep volume steadier than a churn-heavy base chasing only new trial.

Separating “soft” satisfaction from “hard” sales invents a wall the chapter does not draw. Over seasons, the sales line feels whether buyers were content.

Walk a hardware chain: shelves can look full after a promo, but if drills fail in the first month, next quarter’s sales soften as word spreads.

Hardware chains can look busy after a promo while next-quarter sales soften once drills fail in the first month.

So the statement is True.

Satisfaction objectives do not require delighting customers on every dimension before anyone returns. The claim overstates the bar; contentment sufficient to consider repurchase is the practical aim, not perfection on every feature.

All-or-nothing delight rules would make the objective unusable in ordinary markets.

So the statement is False.

Rising customer complaints after a campaign indicate failure on satisfaction objectives, not success. Complaints are a warning that experience missed wishes, even if reach metrics looked strong.

Celebrating complaint spikes as “engagement” misreads the objective the chapter sets.

So the statement is False.

title: Interrelated Marketing Goals
context: Analyze how customer satisfaction interrelates with other marketing objectives such as sales and loyalty. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Businesses analyse customer wishes and needs because unsatisfied buyers will not sustain demand.
Satisfaction objectives aim to convert first-time buyers into customers who return.
A marketing plan that achieves high satisfaction can reinforce market share by retaining buyers.
Satisfied customers never recommend products to others, keeping satisfaction private.
Customer satisfaction is achieved solely by lowering prices below competitors.
tactical_explanations:
Businesses analyse customer wishes and needs because unsatisfied buyers will not sustain demand over time. Listening is not optional decoration; it is how firms avoid building offers nobody wants to repurchase.

So the statement is True.

Satisfaction objectives aim to convert first-time buyers into customers who return. The goal is not a single smile at checkout but a plausible path to the next purchase.

So the statement is True.

A marketing plan that achieves high satisfaction can reinforce market share by retaining buyers who might otherwise switch. Share is relative; keeping your customers while rivals leak theirs moves the needle without only hunting strangers.

Retention from contentment is a share strategy, not a soft alternative to competition.

Picture two coffee chains on one street: the one whose regulars stay because the cup stays good can hold share even when the other spends harder on flyers.

Two coffee chains on one street show it: the cup that keeps regulars can hold share while the rival spends louder on flyers.

So the statement is True.

Satisfied customers often do recommend products to others; satisfaction is not kept private by definition. Word of mouth is a normal spillover from a good experience.

Claiming satisfied buyers “never” recommend invents a silence rule the chapter does not teach.

So the statement is False.

Customer satisfaction is not achieved solely by undercutting competitors on price. Price is one tool; product experience, service, and fit to needs still decide whether buyers feel content.

A race to the bottom can win a trial and still fail satisfaction if the offer disappoints in use.

Undercutting alone can win a trial and still fail satisfaction if the product experience disappoints in use.

Note: cheap can help trial; it is not a complete satisfaction strategy.

So the statement is False.

title: Differentiation Through Branding
context: Consider a hardware store chain comparing local market share, promotional sales spikes, and net profit after covering warehouse costs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Once a customer buys once, satisfaction objectives are automatically fulfilled.
Dissatisfied customers continue buying out of habit, so satisfaction objectives are optional.
Customer satisfaction objectives conflict with profitability and cannot coexist.
Customer complaints rising over time suggest the satisfaction objective is not being achieved.
Satisfaction surveys are irrelevant to assessing marketing objective performance.
tactical_explanations:
One purchase does not automatically fulfil satisfaction objectives forever after. Objectives stay live across use and repurchase; a single checkout is not a lifetime pass.

Post-use surveys and repurchase checks keep satisfaction alive long after a single till receipt fades.

So the statement is False.

Habit alone does not make satisfaction objectives optional for unhappy buyers. Dissatisfied customers may linger briefly, but the chapter does not treat habit as a reason to stop pursuing contentment.

So the statement is False.

Customer satisfaction objectives do not conflict with profitability so badly that they cannot coexist. The chapter treats them as interrelated: content buyers support the repeat revenue that helps profit.

Hardware stores that keep households happy on advice and stock availability often protect margin better than stores that churn through disappointed shoppers.

Framing satisfaction and profit as permanent enemies misreads the objective map.

Profit and satisfaction can share a Monday meeting without cancelling each other in a hardware chain’s scoreboard.

So the statement is False.

Customer complaints rising over time suggest the satisfaction objective is not being achieved. Complaint trends are a direct signal that experience is missing the mark managers claimed to pursue.

A rising complaint curve says the satisfaction aim is slipping even when promotional reach still looks fine.

A rising complaint curve says the satisfaction aim is slipping even when promotional reach still looks fine.

So the statement is True.

Satisfaction surveys are relevant to assessing marketing objective performance because they capture whether buyers feel wishes were met — evidence sales totals alone do not fully show.

Ignoring survey feedback while reviewing “objectives” leaves the satisfaction goal unmeasured.

So the statement is False.

title: Satisfaction and Repeat Purchase
context: Analyze why building a brand supports the creation of a unique selling proposition. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Satisfied customers provide a foundation for brand loyalty programmes to succeed.
If a product fails to meet needs, marketing objectives around sales growth become harder to reach.
A loyal customer is one who buys again regardless of whether they were satisfied.
Satisfaction with product quality can encourage customers to choose the same brand on the next occasion.
Marketing objectives treat customer satisfaction as linked to maintaining competitive sales.
tactical_explanations:
Satisfied customers provide a foundation for brand loyalty programmes to succeed rather than rewarding disappointment. Points and clubs work best when the underlying experience already feels right.

Brand clubs that reward people for staying with a product they dislike create noisy memberships, not chapter-style loyalty.

Brand clubs that reward people for staying with a product they dislike create noisy memberships, not chapter-style loyalty.

So the statement is True.

If a product fails to meet needs, sales-growth objectives get much harder. Volume targets fight uphill when buyers leave unhappy after trial.

So the statement is True.

A loyal customer is not someone who buys again regardless of satisfaction. Loyalty in the chapter’s sense grows from satisfactory experience; blind repurchase after disappointment is not the loyalty objective being taught.

Calling any repeat “loyal” even when the buyer was unhappy empties the word. Brand work and USP aims assume the customer had a reason rooted in contentment.

Blind repurchase after disappointment is not the loyalty objective; contentment is what makes returning make sense.

Blind repurchase after disappointment is not the loyalty objective; contentment is what makes returning make sense.

So the statement is False.

Satisfaction with product quality can encourage customers to choose the same brand on the next occasion, linking contentment to brand preference rather than only to a one-off SKU trial.

That brand-side pull is part of why satisfaction supports differentiation stories.

So the statement is True.

Marketing objectives treat customer satisfaction as linked to maintaining competitive sales. Content buyers return; that continuity helps the firm hold sales against rivals.

Satisfaction is not a museum piece beside the sales target — it feeds it.

So the statement is True.

title: USP and Loyal Customer Attraction
context: Consider a coffee roaster building brand recognition, measuring customer satisfaction scores, and targeting a larger share of the specialty segment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A business measuring repurchase rates is indirectly tracking success on satisfaction objectives.
Customers who feel their wishes were fulfilled are more willing to buy the product again.
Satisfaction objectives complement differentiation by ensuring the promised uniqueness is experienced.
Poor satisfaction can erode market share even when promotional spending remains high.
Satisfaction is an objective because unhappy customers simply will not buy the product again.
tactical_explanations:
Measuring repurchase rates indirectly tracks success on satisfaction objectives, because content buyers are the ones more willing to return. Rising repeats often signal that experience is landing.

Stamp-card renewals at a coffee roaster often echo satisfaction success rather than a separate planet of metrics.

Stamp-card renewals at a coffee roaster often echo satisfaction success rather than a separate planet of metrics.

So the statement is True.

Customers who feel their wishes were fulfilled are more willing to buy the product again. That willingness is the behavioural bridge from satisfaction to volume continuity.

Coffee regulars who got the roast they wanted come back; those who felt misled do not.

So the statement is True.

Satisfaction objectives complement differentiation by ensuring the promised uniqueness is experienced. A USP that looks sharp in ads but feels ordinary in the cup fails the differentiation objective in practice.

Specialty roasters that claim a smoother profile still need satisfaction scores to show guests tasted the difference. Without that lived check, uniqueness stays a slogan.

When guests say the “smoother roast” tasted ordinary, differentiation and satisfaction flash amber together.

So the statement is True.

Poor satisfaction can erode market share even when promotional spending remains high. Ads can recruit trial; dissatisfaction after trial hands those buyers to rivals and softens relative share.

Spend without delivery burns acquisition cash.

So the statement is True.

Satisfaction is an objective because unhappy customers simply will not buy the product again with reliable frequency. Without that repurchase link, sales and loyalty goals become fragile.

Making contentment an explicit aim is how firms protect the next sale, not a decorative CSR line.

So the statement is True.

title: Relative Market Importance
context: Analyze the relationship between higher sales figures and profitability within stated limitations. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Customer satisfaction applies only after market share targets have been reached.
Marketing objectives treat satisfaction as separate from loyalty with no connection.
Loyalty outcomes depend on customers having a satisfactory experience with prior purchases.
Businesses need not fulfil wishes and needs if differentiation is strong enough.
Businesses set satisfaction targets because loyal repeat buyers strengthen several other objectives.
tactical_explanations:
Satisfaction is not something firms pursue only after market share targets are already hit. Listening and contentment work run alongside share aims rather than as a late bonus phase.

Share leaders still survey guests; waiting until share is “done” before caring about contentment is not the objective bundle.

Share leaders still survey guests; waiting until share is “done” before caring about contentment is not the objective bundle.

So the statement is False.

Marketing does not treat satisfaction as sealed off from loyalty with no link. Loyalty outcomes depend on satisfactory prior experience in the chapter’s framework.

So the statement is False.

Loyalty outcomes depend on customers having a satisfactory experience with prior purchases. Points and memberships amplify contentment; they do not replace it.

A retailer can enrol unhappy shoppers in a card scheme and still watch them defect once a rival’s offer feels better. The satisfactory visit is the root; loyalty metrics are the fruit.

: “we have a loyalty programme” is not proof that loyalty objectives are being met if satisfaction is missing.

Enrolment spikes after a poor season do not prove loyalty health if review scores stay ugly.

So the statement is True.

Strong differentiation does not excuse failing to fulfil wishes and needs. A vivid USP that ignores customer needs eventually sells a story buyers do not want to live with.

Differentiation and needs analysis work together, not as substitutes.

So the statement is False.

Businesses set satisfaction targets because loyal repeat buyers strengthen several other objectives — sales continuity, share defence, and the revenue base that supports profit work.

Satisfaction is a hub objective, not an island.

So the statement is True.

title: Sales Covering Production Costs
context: Review why dissatisfied customers are unlikely to buy a product again. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Satisfied customers buy again only when legally required to do so under contract.
Meeting needs analysed in the market helps a firm align its product with satisfaction goals.
Customer satisfaction is unrelated to sales because sales depend only on advertising spend.
A firm with high satisfaction can ignore market share because satisfied buyers guarantee success.
Dissatisfaction improves long-run sales by encouraging customers to try alternatives within the range.
tactical_explanations:
Satisfied customers buy again from preference, not only when a contract forces them. Legal compulsion is not the chapter’s story of how satisfaction supports repurchase.

Preference-driven repeats are what satisfaction tries to earn; contract lock-ins are a different tool entirely.

So the statement is False.

Meeting needs analysed in the market helps a firm align its product with satisfaction goals, so the offering matches what buyers actually wanted rather than what HQ guessed.

Needs work is the map; satisfaction is one destination on it.

So the statement is True.

Customer satisfaction is related to sales; advertising spend alone does not determine volume. Discontented buyers leak even under heavy media weight, while content buyers stretch each campaign’s value through repeats.

Treating sales as a pure advertising function writes satisfaction out of the commercial story the chapter teaches.

If ads alone ruled, firms could ignore product experience forever — which is not the objective framework here.

Heavy ads can fill the funnel while dissatisfaction drains the bottom — sales feel both forces.

Heavy ads can fill the funnel while dissatisfaction drains the bottom — sales feel both forces.

So the statement is False.

High satisfaction does not let a firm ignore market share. Satisfied buyers help, but rivals can still gain relative importance if the firm stops competing for presence and preference in the market.

Satisfaction supports share; it does not guarantee it solo.

So the statement is False.

Dissatisfaction does not improve long-run sales by “encouraging trial of alternatives within the range.” Unhappy customers often leave the firm entirely rather than politely sampling the next SKU.

Burning trust is not a range-architecture strategy. The chapter treats dissatisfaction as a sales risk, not a clever discovery tool.

So the statement is False.

title: Profit Reinvestment Rationale
context: Consider a boutique hotel group emphasising personalised service, measuring guest review scores, and aiming to raise occupancy revenue. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Customer satisfaction objectives are met when promotional reach is high, regardless of product experience.
Satisfied customers never buy complementary products from the same firm.
A satisfied customer base reduces reliance on constant new-customer acquisition alone.
Customer satisfaction is irrelevant to USP objectives because differentiation is purely visual.
Repeat purchase rates falling while satisfaction scores rise always indicates data error only.
tactical_explanations:
High promotional reach does not meet satisfaction objectives if the product experience fails. Reach measures how many people heard the message, not whether guests left content.

Full offer inboxes do not meet satisfaction if boutique rooms disappoint — reach is not guest contentment.

Full offer inboxes do not meet satisfaction if boutique rooms disappoint — reach is not guest contentment.

Guest review scores, not inbox volume, are what tell you whether the satisfaction objective moved.

So the statement is False.

Satisfied customers often do buy complementary products from the same firm. Contentment opens cross-sell; it does not seal buyers into a single SKU forever.

So the statement is False.

A satisfied customer base reduces reliance on constant new-customer acquisition alone. Guests who leave happy return, lifting occupancy revenue without only filling rooms with never-seen-before names.

Boutique hotels that protect review scores often stabilise bookings through repeats and referrals. That is satisfaction doing commercial work, not a soft substitute for revenue targets.

Look at the front desk: a returning guest costs less to win than a cold lead from a flash promo.

Returning guests cost less than cold promo leads; review scores that protect repeats shrink acquisition dependence.

So the statement is True.

Customer satisfaction is relevant to USP objectives because differentiation must be experienced, not merely visual. A craftsmanship story that fails in use undercuts the unique selling claim.

Visual polish without lived difference does not finish the USP job.

So the statement is False.

Falling repeat rates while satisfaction scores rise is not always “data error only.” Timing lags, segment mixes, or competitor shocks can separate the series without proving the survey is nonsense.

Managers should investigate, not assume the only explanation is broken data.

So the statement is False.

title: Dissatisfaction and Lost Sales
context: Review the marketing objective of maintaining sales volume to generate revenue. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Customer satisfaction is one of several marketing objectives a business may pursue.
Satisfaction contributes to profitability indirectly by supporting repeat revenue streams.
When customers are satisfied, they are more likely to remain with the firm rather than switch.
Customer satisfaction means the product must be the cheapest in the market.
Marketing staff may track satisfaction scores alongside sales when reviewing objective performance.
tactical_explanations:
Customer satisfaction sits among several marketing objectives a business may pursue — alongside sales, share, profit, and differentiation aims rather than as a lone goal.

Satisfaction sits among several aims; crowning it as the only goal would erase sales and profit from the same list.

Satisfaction sits among several aims; crowning it as the only goal would erase sales and profit from the same list.

Satisfaction sits among several aims; crowning it as the only goal would erase sales and profit from the same list.

So the statement is True.

Satisfaction contributes to profitability indirectly by supporting repeat revenue streams that keep volume covering costs and feeding surplus. Content buyers return; that continuity helps the profit story.

So the statement is True.

When customers are satisfied, they are more likely to remain with the firm rather than switch, which is why dissatisfaction shows up later as lost sales and weaker loyalty metrics.

Retention is the commercial face of contentment. A bakery that keeps regulars because the loaf stays good does not need to win every stranger on the street each morning.

A bakery keeping regulars because the loaf stays good shows retention as the commercial face of contentment.

So the statement is True.

Customer satisfaction does not mean the product must be the cheapest in the market. Contentment can rest on quality, service, fit, or reliability while price sits elsewhere in the mix.

Cheapest-wins is a pricing claim, not the definition of satisfaction.

So the statement is False.

Marketing staff may track satisfaction scores alongside sales when reviewing objective performance, because the two move together in the framework and each illuminates the other.

Joint dashboards are ordinary practice, not a category error.

So the statement is True.

title: Perceived Product Uniqueness
context: Analyze how retained profit from higher sales can be reinvested in the business. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Loyalty programmes eliminate the need to pursue customer satisfaction objectives.
Dissatisfied customers still generate loyal behaviour if enrolled in a rewards scheme.
A product that delights customers on first use is better positioned to achieve loyalty objectives.
Customer satisfaction is a financial accounting measure identical to gross profit.
Businesses set satisfaction objectives only in declining markets.
tactical_explanations:
Loyalty programmes do not remove the need to pursue satisfaction objectives. Cards and points amplify a good experience; they do not excuse a bad one.

A rewards app on a disappointing product mostly reminds customers how often they regretted the purchase.

So the statement is False.

Rewards enrolment does not turn dissatisfied buyers into truly loyal ones. Points cannot paper over a product that failed the customer’s wishes.

So the statement is False.

A product that delights customers on first use is better positioned to achieve loyalty objectives because the initial experience gives loyalty schemes something real to reinforce.

First-use delight plants the memory; membership then rewards returning to it. Starting loyalty mechanics before the product lands leaves the programme promoting disappointment.

Picture a new snack line: the first bite decides whether the app’s stamp card ever gets used twice.

First-bite delight on a snack line decides whether the stamp card ever gets used twice.

So the statement is True.

Customer satisfaction is not a financial accounting measure identical to gross profit. It is a marketing objective about whether buyers feel wishes were met, tracked with surveys and behaviour — not a P&L line equal to gross profit.

Conflating the two mixes scoreboards.

So the statement is False.

Businesses set satisfaction objectives in growing and stable markets as well as declining ones. Limiting satisfaction goals to decline phases invents a timing rule the chapter does not teach.

Contentment matters whenever firms want repeats.

So the statement is False.

title: Share Maintenance Strategies
context: Consider a regional bakery that tracks repeat purchases, complaint rates, and promotional responses while setting annual marketing targets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A satisfied customer will never switch to a rival with a stronger USP.
Customer satisfaction objectives are fulfilled when production volume is maximised.

tactical_explanations:
Even a satisfied customer may switch if a rival offers a stronger USP. Contentment helps retention; it is not an unbreakable lock against better-perceived alternatives.

So the statement is False.

Maximising production volume does not by itself fulfil satisfaction objectives. Making more units says nothing about whether buyers felt their wishes were met.

Factories can run flat out while customers still feel ignored — volume and satisfaction are different scoreboards.

Factories can run flat out while customers still feel ignored — volume and satisfaction are different scoreboards.

Baking more loaves than last year says nothing about whether households felt the promised crust.

So the statement is False.

A unique selling proposition does not mean the product is identical to all similar products on every feature — that claim reverses the idea. A USP is the meaningful difference buyers recognise, not sameness across the board.

If every feature matched rivals, there would be nothing unique to sell. Differentiation work hunts a gap customers care about, whether in recipe, service, or brand story.

Promo spikes without satisfaction leak away.

Promise–delivery alignment is how differentiation and satisfaction reinforce each other.

title: Better Than the Rest Positioning
context: Consider a regional bakery that tracks repeat purchases, complaint rates, and promotional responses while setting annual marketing targets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Market share reflects how much of the market's total sales the firm captures.
Competitiveness improves when a firm gains share while rivals lose ground.
Share targets are set after analysing the market the business wants to operate in.
A firm with declining satisfaction may see market share fall as customers switch.
Marketing objectives on share align with wanting a certain portion of market sales.
tactical_explanations:
Market share is the bakery's slice of what the whole catchment buys — loaves, pastries, cakes — not a medal hanging beside the ovens. When managers add the firm's sales and divide by total category sales in that market, the percentage is the share. The statement is naming that portion idea cleanly.

So the statement is True.

Competitiveness is a relative story, not a solo revenue chart. If the regional bakery climbs from twelve to fifteen percent while two supermarket in-store bakeries slip, buyers are shifting toward you. Gaining share while rivals lose ground is exactly the movement the chapter treats as stronger competitive standing — stronger than merely selling more in an expanding pie where everyone grows together and nobody's slice really changes.

So the statement is True.

Share targets are not invented in a vacuum after a brainstorm sticky-note. The bakery first maps which market it wants — weekday bread, weekend cakes, catering trays — and only then writes a realistic slice goal. Setting the percentage after that market analysis is how the overview sequences planning.

So the statement is True.

Look at the complaint sheet and the share chart together. When satisfaction slides — stale crust, cold coffee, slow queues — regulars drift to the rival two streets over. Declining satisfaction often shows up later as a thinner market share because switching is how unhappy buyers vote. The statement links those two outcomes correctly for a firm that tracks both.

A bakery that ignores rising complaints while celebrating last quarter's volume is blindsiding itself: the share loss is already brewing in the feedback. Satisfaction is not soft colour on a poster; it protects the slice against rivals who are waiting for one bad batch.

So the statement is True.

Marketing objectives on share are simply the wish to hold or grow a defined portion of market sales. The bakery that says "we want eighteen percent of specialty bread in the region" is writing a share objective in the textbook sense — a portion target, not a vague hope to "do well" somehow.

So the statement is True.

title: Relative Not Absolute Share
context: Review relative share metrics when comparing firms of different absolute sales sizes. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Industry reports ranking firms by share illustrate relative importance.
Sales objectives are independent of market analysis of wishes and needs.
A firm with rising sales never needs to monitor production costs.
Sales volume objectives are achieved when warehouse stock levels peak.
Revenue coverage of costs is irrelevant when pursuing differentiation objectives.
tactical_explanations:
Industry league tables that rank firms by share are teaching relative importance: who weighs more in the market, not who has the tallest warehouse. A mid-sized specialist can outrank a larger generalist inside a narrow category because share is always relative to the defined field.

So the statement is True.

Sales objectives sit on top of market analysis of wishes and needs. You cannot set a meaningful volume target while pretending buyers' preferences are irrelevant. The claim that sales goals are independent of that analysis severs the planning sequence the chapter insists on.

Picture a furniture retailer guessing a huge sofa target without asking what households want from craftsmanship or delivery. The number floats free of demand. Independence from needs work is the trap, not the method.

So the statement is False.

Rising sales do not retire the cost clipboard. Volume can climb while unit costs, waste, or overtime quietly erase the gain. A firm that celebrates revenue and never monitors production costs is running half a dashboard. The "never needs to monitor" claim is false under any healthy sales story.

: sales growth and cost control travel together toward profit. Dropping cost attention because invoices look busy is how busy firms still lose money. Rising sales are a reason to watch costs more carefully, not less — especially when overtime and waste scale with throughput.

So the statement is False.

Warehouse stock peaking is inventory sitting on pallets, not sales success. Sales volume objectives care about what customers purchase and pay for, not how high the forklift stacks the aisle. A full storeroom with weak sell-through misses the sales goal even if the warehouse looks "productive".

So the statement is False.

Differentiation does not cancel the need for revenue to cover costs. A craftsmanship-led furniture line still has to pay timber, wages, and freight from sales receipts. Calling cost coverage irrelevant while chasing a USP invents a free lunch the chapter does not offer.

Note: uniqueness can support better prices, but it never replaces the sales-to-cost arithmetic managers still have to do.

So the statement is False.

title: Ongoing Revenue From Sales
context: Analyze the sales-profit relationship subject to cost and pricing constraints. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Defensive marketing aims to stop share loss to aggressive competitors.
Share and sales objectives together give absolute and relative performance views.
A competitiveness review typically examines market share alongside rival trends.
Gaining share in a mature market often requires taking customers from established rivals.
Market share is an indicator, not a substitute for profitability analysis.
tactical_explanations:
Defensive marketing is the hold-the-line play: stop aggressive rivals from peeling away your share. It is not about inventing a new category overnight; it is about protecting the slice you already have when competitors push promotions, prices, or shiny new offers at your regulars.

So the statement is True.

Share and sales objectives work as a pair of lenses on the same business. Sales give the absolute euros or units moved; share shows how that absolute stacks up against rivals in the field. Managers who only watch one miss either the size of the operation or its competitive weight. Using both is the overview's dual performance view — absolute activity plus relative standing in one planning conversation.

So the statement is True.

A competitiveness review without share sitting next to rival trends is mostly storytelling. Putting your percentage beside competitors' movements is the standard comparative reading — who gained, who slipped, and whether your standing improved this quarter versus the names that actually matter.

So the statement is True.

In a mature market the pie barely grows, so a larger slice usually means someone else's customers moved. Gaining share then often means winning switchers from established rivals — loyalty cards, sharper offers, better service windows — not waiting for brand-new demand to appear from nowhere.

If that were not true, mature categories would hand free growth to every entrant without displacing incumbents. The chapter's mature-market logic is switching pressure, not magic expansion of the total. Defensive rivals know this, which is why share fights get sharp when growth stalls.

So the statement is True.

Market share is a useful indicator of relative standing, not a substitute for profitability analysis. You can lead on share and still miss margin targets if costs or deep discounts run wild. Keep both reviews on the management agenda rather than treating the slice as the whole scoreboard.

So the statement is True.

title: Internal Fund Retention
context: Consider a furniture retailer that surveys post-purchase satisfaction, promotes a craftsmanship guarantee, and aims to grow regional sales volume. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Sales growth from dissatisfied one-time buyers is a sustainable long-run strategy.
Businesses monitor share because it shows position relative to competitors' positions.
Unit sales targets are unrelated to quarterly marketing planning.
Sales are unconnected to profitability because profit comes only from asset sales.
Maintaining sales means prices must rise every month regardless of demand.
tactical_explanations:
Chasing volume from buyers who leave unhappy is a short sugar rush, not a long-run strategy. Dissatisfied one-time purchasers do not become the repeat base a furniture retailer needs for sustainable sales growth. The statement sells a leaky bucket as a plan.

So the statement is False.

Businesses watch share because it shows where they sit relative to competitors' positions in the same market. Absolute sales alone cannot tell you whether you are gaining or losing ground when rivals move too. The comparative reading is the point of the indicator.

A furniture retailer comparing itself only to last year's own receipts can feel successful while a craftsmanship rival quietly takes the high street. Share puts those two positions on one map. Relative placement is the reason the indicator earns a place in marketing talk.

So the statement is True.

Unit sales targets belong inside quarterly marketing planning — they are not an optional side hobby. Campaign calendars, stock orders, and staff rotas all lean on those volume numbers. Calling them unrelated to the quarter's plan misreads how marketing planning actually works on the floor.

Quarterly calendars without unit targets leave buying, staffing, and promo timing guessing. The sales number is what the quarter's marketing plan hangs coats on. Unrelatedness would mean planning without a volume stake — which is not how serious retail quarters run.

So the statement is False.

Sales and profitability are tightly linked: revenue from selling furniture is what covers costs before any profit appears. Pretending profit comes only from selling off assets — dumping vans or warehouse space — ignores the ordinary trading path the chapter describes. Asset disposals are not the routine profit engine.

Walk a craftsmanship-led retailer: sofas sold this month fund wages and timber invoices; that is the sales-to-profit bridge. Treating sales as "unconnected" because someone once sold a forklift invents a false exception as the rule.

Note: occasional asset sales can create a one-off gain, but that is not how marketing objectives frame ongoing profitability.

So the statement is False.

Maintaining sales does not mean cranking prices up every month no matter what demand does. Price hikes that ignore willingness to pay can shrink volume and wreck the very sales level you meant to protect. Demand still sets the ceiling.

So the statement is False.

title: Single Objective Trap Cases
context: Analyze unique selling propositions that rest on delivery speed, design, or service elements. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A marketing objective to grow share implies outperforming rivals in relative terms.
A promotional campaign that raises awareness but not purchases meets sales objectives.
Sales volume is measured by the number of employees rather than customer purchases.
Share maintenance can be supported by customer loyalty built through satisfaction.
Relative importance in the market is the concept market share is meant to convey.
tactical_explanations:
Growing share is a relative ambition: you are aiming to weigh more in the market than before, which means outperforming rivals on that comparative yardstick. Absolute sales can rise while share falls; a share-growth objective is specifically about beating that relative race.

So the statement is True.

Awareness without purchases does not meet sales objectives. Knowing the brand exists is not the same as buying the chair, the cream, or the coffee. A campaign that only lifts recognition while tills stay quiet fails the sales test the chapter uses.

So the statement is False.

Sales volume is counted from what customers buy, not from how many people work in the shop. Headcount is a staffing metric; purchases are the sales metric. Mixing those two invents a nonsense measure of volume.

So the statement is False.

Share maintenance leans hard on loyalty, and loyalty usually grows from satisfaction. Buyers who liked the last delivery, the fit, or the aftercare come back — and that repeat behaviour holds the slice when rivals advertise. Satisfaction → loyalty → defended share is the chain the statement sketches.

Picture a furniture floor where post-purchase surveys stay green and craftsmanship guarantees are honoured: those households are less likely to defect when a discounter opens nearby. The share defence is already half-built in the experience.

Loyalty from satisfaction is the quiet share defence: buyers who were treated well do not sample every new delivery-speed or design USP that appears. Maintenance is easier when the experience already glued customers in place before the next rival campaign.

So the statement is True.

Market share exists to convey relative importance in the market — how heavy the firm is compared with others serving the same field. It is not a warehouse-size medal or a raw euro total read in isolation. Relative weight is the concept the indicator is built for, and the statement names that purpose correctly rather than confusing share with absolute scale alone.

Ask "who matters more in this market?" and share is the answer the overview wants — not square metres of warehouse or a lone euro total without a denominator. Relative importance is the job description of the share figure.

So the statement is True.

title: USP Misclassification Traps
context: Review market share erosion as a signal of weakened competitive position. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Maintaining or increasing sales is a marketing objective because sales generate revenue.
Increasing sales is impossible when pursuing customer satisfaction objectives.
Sales revenue cannot fund production costs if the product is differentiated.
Sales are important to businesses because revenues must cover production costs.
A business with zero sales can still meet sales volume objectives through forecasts.
tactical_explanations:
Maintaining or increasing sales sits among marketing objectives because sales are what generate the revenue stream. Without that inflow, the rest of the plan — promotions, stock, service — has nothing commercial to stand on. The statement's "because" clause is exactly the textbook reason.

So the statement is True.

Customer satisfaction and higher sales are allies, not enemies. Satisfied buyers tend to repurchase, which lifts volume over time. Claiming that pursuing satisfaction makes sales increases impossible invents a false conflict the overview does not teach.

So the statement is False.

Differentiation does not freeze sales revenue out of the cost-coverage job. A differentiated product still sells, and those receipts still pay for production. Saying differentiated goods cannot fund costs from sales misreads both differentiation and the sales-cost link.

So the statement is False.

Sales matter because the money customers pay has to cover what it costs to make and deliver the offer. That coverage logic is why volume and revenue sit in the marketing objectives conversation rather than as optional vanity counts. Activity without cost coverage is theatre.

A cosmetics launch can look busy in the press and still fail if revenue never catches production and marketing spend. The statement keeps the eye on that commercial necessity.

When share is eroding, the revenue-coverage reminder gets sharper: you still need sales to pay for making the product even while you fight for position. Importance of sales is not cancelled by a competitiveness scare; it is why the scare hurts.

So the statement is True.

Forecasts are plans, not sales. A business with zero actual sales has not met a sales volume objective merely by writing optimistic numbers on a spreadsheet. Objectives are judged by realised purchases, not by hope in a forecast file.

Note: forecasts help set targets; they do not substitute for recorded volume when you ask whether the sales objective was achieved.

Zero tills plus a beautiful forecast slide is still a miss. Sales volume objectives ask what actually moved, not what the planning pack hoped would move. Forecasts guide; they do not score the objective as achieved.

So the statement is False.

title: Share Versus Absolute Sales
context: Consider a cosmetics firm launching a premium skincare range with a clear differentiation message and tracking customer repurchase rates. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Sales revenue contributes to the ability to make a profit after costs are met.
A business pursuing higher sales aims to strengthen its revenue inflow.
Marketing campaigns often target a sales volume increase in a defined period.
Sales objectives replace the need for any profitability analysis.
Sales objectives may be stated in units sold or in revenue terms.
tactical_explanations:
Sales revenue is the pool from which costs are paid before any profit can appear. After production and related costs are met, what remains can be profit. The statement correctly places revenue as a contributor to that profit possibility, not as profit itself.

So the statement is True.

Pursuing higher sales is a push to strengthen the revenue inflow — more units, more invoices, more cash coming in from customers. That is the straightforward commercial aim behind a sales-growth objective in the marketing overview.

So the statement is True.

Campaigns often carry an explicit volume lift for a defined window — this quarter, this launch month, this seasonal peak. Marketing activity is frequently aimed at moving that sales needle inside a clear time box rather than floating forever without a target date.

A premium skincare launch week with a written unit lift is doing exactly that: campaign energy aimed at a dated volume increase. Without the period box, "more sales someday" never becomes a checkable marketing objective.

So the statement is True.

Sales objectives never retire profitability analysis. You can hit volume and still miss profit if margins collapse or costs spike. Treating sales targets as a full replacement for profit review is the single-objective trap the chapter warns against.

Walk a premium skincare launch: unit sales can look strong while heavy sampling, returns, or discounting erase the surplus. Managers still need the profitability lens beside the sales chart. Volume success is necessary material for profit, not a certificate that profit work is finished.

Repurchase rates can look healthy while sampling costs and trade discounts hollow out the surplus. That is why profitability analysis stays on the desk after sales objectives are written. Replacement of profit review by volume alone is the trap.

So the statement is False.

Sales objectives can be written in units — jars, bottles, kits — or in revenue euros. Both are legitimate ways to state what "higher sales" means for the period. The firm picks the language that matches how it plans and measures the campaign.

So the statement is True.

title: Profit Without Sales Trap
context: Review profit reinvestment as a strategic use of earnings retained in the business. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Without adequate sales, a business cannot cover its production costs from revenue.
Increasing sales is listed among marketing objectives businesses may pursue.
Seasonal sales peaks may still align with an overall objective to increase annual volume.
Revenue from exports does not count toward sales volume objectives.
Sales growth supports cash inflows needed for day-to-day operations.
tactical_explanations:
Without enough sales, there is no revenue stream large enough to cover production costs. Factories, kitchens, and warehouses do not pay for themselves from good intentions. The statement is the plain cost-coverage truth the overview starts from.

So the statement is True.

Increasing sales is on the list of marketing objectives businesses may chase — alongside satisfaction, share, differentiation, and profit. It is not an outsider metric smuggled in from accounting; it belongs in the marketing objective set the chapter names.

So the statement is True.

A summer spike and a quiet January can still sit under one annual volume objective. Seasonal peaks are timing, not a separate philosophy. Hitting a higher yearly total often uses those peaks rather than fighting them. Alignment between seasonal rhythm and the annual increase goal is normal planning.

Annual volume goals often ride seasonal waves rather than fighting them — peak weeks bank progress toward the year target. A summer rush that serves the annual increase is alignment, not a contradiction of the yearly objective.

So the statement is True.

Export revenue is still sales. Units or euros sold abroad count toward sales volume objectives just as domestic tills do. Excluding exports invents a border the marketing overview does not draw around "real" sales.

Picture a coffee roaster shipping bags to neighbouring countries: those invoices are sales volume, not a different species of money. Period targets include that channel unless the plan explicitly carves it out — and the statement's blanket exclusion is wrong.

Note: firms may set separate domestic and export targets, but export revenue still counts as sales toward the objectives that include it.

So the statement is False.

Sales growth feeds the cash inflows that keep day-to-day operations moving — paying suppliers, wages, and routine bills. Stronger volume usually means a stronger operating cash pulse, which is why growth objectives matter beyond bragging rights.

So the statement is True.

title: Satisfaction Isolation Errors
context: Analyze the objective hierarchy in which satisfaction supports loyalty and subsequent sales. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Higher sales figures always reduce production costs per unit to zero.
A promotional discount may be used to lift short-term sales volume.
Sales growth objectives are unrelated to customer loyalty from satisfaction.
A temporary sales spike from a failed product satisfies long-term sales objectives.
Sales targets are set after analysing the market the firm wishes to serve.
tactical_explanations:
Higher sales never magic production costs per unit down to zero. Scale can help unit costs fall, but materials, labour, and overhead do not vanish. The "always… to zero" claim is an absolute the chapter does not support.

So the statement is False.

A short promotional discount is a classic lever for lifting near-term sales volume — a weekend offer, a launch price, a bundle. It may not be the whole strategy, but it is a recognised tool for a temporary volume bump when the plan calls for one.

So the statement is True.

Sales growth and loyalty from satisfaction are related, not sealed in separate rooms. Satisfied loyal buyers are often the most reliable path to sustained volume. Calling growth objectives unrelated to that loyalty chain cuts the hierarchy the overview describes.

Loyalty born of satisfaction is often the cheapest path to durable sales growth. Treating growth aims as sealed off from that loyalty chain asks volume to appear without the buyers who stick. The hierarchy links them on purpose.

So the statement is False.

A one-week spike on a product that then fails does not satisfy long-term sales objectives. Sustainable volume needs repeatable demand, not a fireworks chart that collapses. Temporary excitement is not the same as meeting the lasting sales aim.

If that spike were enough, every flash promo on a dud SKU would count as strategic success.

Long-term sales objectives care about whether demand survives the hangover. A failed product's temporary spike teaches almost nothing about sustained volume. Fireworks are not a substitute for a lasting sales path.

So the statement is False.

Sales targets follow analysis of the market the firm wants to serve. You read wishes, needs, and demand shape first, then write numbers that fit that field. Targets before market reading are guesses with letterhead.

So the statement is True.

title: Differentiation Definition Traps
context: Consider a coffee roaster building brand recognition, measuring customer satisfaction scores, and targeting a larger share of the specialty segment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Revenue from sales must exceed production costs for profit to be possible.
Maintaining sales volume can be an objective when a market matures.
Sales performance is monitored to assess progress toward marketing objectives.
A decline in unit sales may signal failure on sales-related marketing objectives.
Higher sales figures usually support profitability, subject to stated limitations.
tactical_explanations:
Profit only becomes possible when sales revenue clears production costs. If costs sit above what customers paid, there is no surplus to call profit. The statement restates that necessary inequality in plain commercial language.

So the statement is True.

When a market matures and easy growth fades, simply maintaining sales volume can itself be the marketing objective — hold the line on units or revenue while the category flattens. Defence of volume is a real goal, not only aggressive expansion.

So the statement is True.

Managers monitor sales performance to see whether marketing objectives are being met. Charts of units and revenue are progress checks against the plan, not decorative dashboards. The monitoring habit is how sales objectives stay honest.

So the statement is True.

Falling unit sales is a warning light on sales-related objectives. If the plan said grow or even hold volume, a decline is evidence of miss — not a quirky success signal. The statement reads that signal the way marketers should.

A coffee roaster targeting specialty-segment volume who watches bags-per-week slide should treat that as a sales-objective problem: distribution, satisfaction, or the USP story may need work. Ignoring the decline because "brand feel" still looks warm is how objectives quietly fail.

Specialty coffee bags sliding week after week while the brand story still sounds warm is a sales-objective miss in progress. Declining units are the signal; pretending otherwise protects feelings, not the plan.

So the statement is True.

Higher sales usually help profitability — more revenue to work with — but only subject to the limitations the chapter flags: costs, discounts, and mix can still spoil the ending. The "usually… subject to limitations" wording matches that careful link.

Keep the limitations in the same sentence as the optimism: higher sales help profit until costs or discounts say otherwise. The chapter's careful link is tendency plus caveat, which this wording preserves.

So the statement is True.

title: Market Share Purpose Errors
context: Analyze share maintenance when entering mature markets with established competitors. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Sales objectives interrelate with customer satisfaction because repeat buyers add volume.
Distribution expansion may be pursued to increase sales to new geographic areas.
A firm may set quarterly sales targets as part of its marketing plan.
Sales are important because they allow the firm to ignore market share completely.
Sales volume growth in a new product launch is a common marketing objective.
tactical_explanations:
Sales objectives and satisfaction interlock because satisfied customers come back, and repeat purchases add volume. Cut satisfaction and you eventually cut the sales engine. The statement names that repeat-buyer bridge correctly.

So the statement is True.

Opening new distribution — another region, another channel, another city — is a standard route to higher sales. Geographic reach brings new buyers into the volume count. Pursuing expansion for that reason is ordinary marketing planning, not a side quest.

New depots, new cities, new retail partners — distribution expansion is how volume reaches buyers who could not buy before. Geographic reach is a sales lever, not a logistics hobby detached from marketing objectives.

So the statement is True.

Quarterly sales targets are everyday furniture in a marketing plan. Firms break the year into checkpoints so campaigns, stock, and reviews have a rhythm. Setting those targets is part of how the plan becomes operational.

So the statement is True.

Sales importance does not licence ignoring market share. Volume and relative standing answer different questions; strong sales can still hide share loss if rivals grow faster. The claim that sales let you scrap share entirely is the false either-or.

In a mature market with established competitors, managers often watch both: absolute orders and the slice versus named rivals. Dropping share from the dashboard because tills rang this month is how competitive slippage sneaks in. Sales matter; they do not retire the relative lens.

In a mature field with named incumbents, share still tells you whether your sales success is competitive or just floating with the tide. Ignoring share because sales feel busy is how relative decline hides inside absolute comfort.

So the statement is False.

Launching a new product commonly carries a sales volume growth objective for the introduction window. Getting early units moving is a classic marketing aim when something new hits the shelf.

Without that early volume stake, a launch plan risks celebrating awareness while the product sits. The introduction window is exactly when sales objectives earn their place beside the brand story.

So the statement is True.

title: Sales Alone Sufficiency Traps
context: Review revenue growth objectives tied to covering fixed and variable production costs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Maintaining sales requires shutting down marketing expenditure entirely.
Sales volume and revenue are unrelated concepts in the marketing objectives framework.
Production costs are covered from government grants rather than sales revenue.
Revenue coverage of costs is why sales matter beyond mere activity measures.
Wholesale and retail channels both contribute to the firm's total sales volume.
tactical_explanations:
Maintaining sales usually needs marketing spend — reminders, promotions, presence — not a total shutdown of the budget. Cutting every marketing euro is a fast way to watch volume fade, not a recipe for holding it. The statement gets the expenditure logic backwards.

So the statement is False.

Sales volume and sales revenue are related ideas in the objectives framework: volume is how many; revenue is volume times price. Calling them unrelated invents a split the chapter does not teach. Managers use both languages when they write sales aims.

So the statement is False.

Production costs are covered from sales revenue in the ordinary commercial model, not from government grants as a default. Grants may appear in special cases, but the marketing overview's cost-coverage story runs through what customers pay. The statement swaps the main path for an exception.

Grants may appear in odd cases, but the marketing overview's default story is customers paying and that revenue covering production. Swapping the default for government funding as the normal cover path misstates the commercial model.

So the statement is False.

Sales matter beyond mere activity counts because revenue has to cover costs. Busy shelves and busy ads are not enough if the money never clears production. That coverage reason is why sales sit among serious marketing objectives rather than as a vanity footfall tally.

Walk a firm chasing fixed and variable cost cover: every euro of sales revenue is doing cost work before profit talk even starts. The statement keeps that purpose in view.

Activity metrics — footfall, impressions, meetings — can look alive while costs go unpaid. Sales matter because they are the revenue that does the coverage work. That is the step beyond mere busyness.

So the statement is True.

Wholesale shipments and retail sell-through both feed the firm's total sales volume when those channels are how the product reaches buyers. Counting only one while ignoring the other understates the commercial total the objectives track.

So the statement is True.

title: Profitability Link Misstatements
context: Consider a boutique hotel group emphasising personalised service, measuring guest review scores, and aiming to raise occupancy revenue. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Increasing sales means profitability objectives become unnecessary.
A sales objective to maintain volume may apply when supply constraints cap growth.
Sales objectives are fulfilled when distribution centres are built, regardless of sell-through.
Marketing spend on advertising may aim to raise sales of a specific product line.
A firm can make a profit without any sales if customer satisfaction is high.
tactical_explanations:
Higher sales never make profitability objectives unnecessary. Volume without margin still fails owners and reinvestment needs. A boutique hotel can fill rooms and miss profit if discounts and service costs eat the rate. Sales growth and profit aims travel together; one does not cancel the other.

A full boutique hotel with razor rates and heavy service cost can miss profit while sales look triumphant. Volume never retires the profitability objective; the two stay on the same management agenda for a reason.

So the statement is False.

When supply is capped — full occupancy, limited rooms, fixed kitchen capacity — a sales objective may simply be to maintain volume rather than chase impossible growth. Holding the achievable level is still a real marketing target under constraint.

So the statement is True.

Building distribution centres is logistics investment, not sales fulfilment. Sales objectives are met when customers buy, not when warehouses open. Sell-through is the test; bricks and racking are only enablers.

So the statement is False.

Advertising spend is often aimed at lifting sales of a named line — a room package, a spa offer, a seasonal stay. Linking budget to a specific product's sales is ordinary marketing targeting, not wasteful noise. The statement describes that aim correctly.

So the statement is True.

High guest satisfaction does not create profit without sales. Reviews can glow while the hotel stays empty; without bookings there is no revenue to cover costs or yield surplus. Satisfaction supports repeat sales — it does not replace them.

Note: satisfaction and sales reinforce each other, but "profit with zero sales" breaks the revenue arithmetic the chapter uses.

Glowing reviews with empty books still leave no revenue. Satisfaction is a path toward repeat sales, not a spare generator that prints profit without bookings. Zero sales, high scores, no surplus — the arithmetic does not bend.

So the statement is False.

title: Loyalty Without Satisfaction
context: Review post-purchase satisfaction as a predictor of whether customers return. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Unit sales growth contributes to the revenue pool from which costs are paid.
Profitability is unrelated to sales because profits come only from borrowed funds.
Higher sales always reduce profit because production costs rise infinitely with volume.
Profits cannot be retained in the business for reinvestment under any circumstances.
Sales data helps managers see whether marketing objectives are being achieved.
tactical_explanations:
Unit sales growth widens the revenue pool that pays for production and related costs. More units sold, at a price, means more money available for that coverage job. The statement places growth in that funding role correctly.

So the statement is True.

Profitability is not unrelated to sales, and profits do not come "only from borrowed funds." Borrowing is finance; profit is what remains after sales revenue covers costs. Treating sales as irrelevant to profit reverses the commercial sequence.

So the statement is False.

Higher sales do not always reduce profit, and production costs do not rise "infinitely" with volume in any useful model. Costs may rise, but revenue rises too; the net depends on margins. Absolute doom-from-volume is a cartoon, not the chapter's limitation language.

Infinite cost growth with volume is a cartoon. Real limitations talk about costs rising and margins shifting — not about profit always dying whenever sales rise. The absolute doom claim oversells the warning into nonsense.

So the statement is False.

Profits can be retained and reinvested — that is a standard use of earnings kept in the business. Saying retention is impossible "under any circumstances" contradicts the overview's reinvestment story. Owners may withdraw some profit and leave the rest inside; both happen.

If retention were banned, firms could never fund growth from their own surplus. The chapter treats plough-back as normal strategy, not as a forbidden move.

Plough-back of profit into better service or stock is how firms fund tomorrow from today's surplus. Banning retention "under any circumstances" would freeze that path. The overview treats reinvestment as available, not forbidden.

So the statement is False.

Sales data is how managers check whether marketing objectives are landing — volume against plan, revenue against target. Without those figures, "are we achieving the sales aim?" is guesswork. Monitoring sales is the feedback loop for those objectives.
