So the statement is True.

title: Brand Versus USP Confusion
context: Analyze promotional differentiation that shapes how customers classify the product mentally. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A business with rising sales but rising costs may still miss profit objectives.
Profitability objectives exclude owner reimbursement for invested capital.
Marketing objectives never include profitability because marketing only targets awareness.
A firm with falling sales can always increase profit without any cost changes.
Retained profit is identical to short-term trade credit from suppliers.
tactical_explanations:
Rising sales with rising costs can still miss profit objectives. If cost growth outruns revenue growth, the surplus shrinks or vanishes even while the top line looks healthy. Volume alone never guarantees the profit target.

So the statement is True.

Profitability objectives include reimbursing owners for capital they invested — that return is part of why profit matters. Excluding owner reimbursement from the profit aim cuts out a reason the chapter explicitly gives for caring about profit.

So the statement is False.

Marketing objectives do include profitability; marketing is not limited to awareness metrics. Awareness may be a tactic or interim measure, but the objective set still reaches toward profitable commercial outcomes. "Never include profitability" is too narrow a cage.

Awareness can be a campaign metric; profitability remains in the marketing objective set. Narrowing marketing to awareness-only goals leaves owners and reinvestment without a seat. The "never include profit" cage is too small.

So the statement is False.

Falling sales do not "always" raise profit with zero cost changes. Less volume usually means less revenue; without cost cuts, profit typically weakens, not strengthens. The claim invents an automatic profit win from decline that arithmetic does not deliver.

Walk a firm whose orders drop while rent, wages, and materials stay put: the surplus is under pressure. Profit recovery would need cost action or price repair — not faith that lower sales magically enrich the owners.

Orders fall, costs stay put, surplus usually shrinks. Automatic profit from declining sales without cost cuts contradicts ordinary arithmetic. The claim needs cost action it refuses to allow — so it fails.

So the statement is False.

Retained profit is earnings kept in the business; short-term trade credit is money owed to suppliers for goods. They are different financing ideas. Equating plough-back with supplier credit mixes ownership surplus with a payable.

So the statement is False.

title: Competitor Share Comparisons
context: Review competitive benchmarking through market share alongside sales and profit trends. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Maintaining sales is essential for ongoing revenue to fund business activity.
Profitability and sales objectives are completely unrelated measures.
Sales objectives complement share objectives by measuring absolute performance.
Owners are reimbursed through sales volume alone without any profit calculation.
Promotional bundles may be introduced to stimulate higher sales volume quickly.
tactical_explanations:
Maintaining sales keeps the revenue flowing that funds day-to-day business activity — suppliers, staff, routine operations. Let volume collapse and that funding pulse weakens. Essential is the right word for sales' role in ongoing commercial life.

So the statement is True.

Profitability and sales objectives are related, not sealed off from each other. Sales supply the revenue base; profit asks what remains after costs. Calling them "completely unrelated" denies the link the overview keeps stressing, including its limitations.

So the statement is False.

Sales objectives complement share objectives: share is relative weight; sales are absolute performance. A firm can watch both — how many units, and what slice of the market those units represent. Complementary measurement is the point, not rivalry between the two aims.

Absolute sales say how big you are; share says how you weigh against rivals. Writing both objectives is complementary measurement. They answer different questions on the same competitive field.

So the statement is True.

Owners are not reimbursed by raw sales volume alone. Reimbursement runs through profit — what is left after costs — not through ringing tills without a surplus calculation. Volume without profit does not pay owners for invested capital in the sense the chapter means.

Note: strong sales help create the chance of profit, but the reimbursement story is profit-based, not volume-as-paycheck.

Tills ringing without a surplus do not reimburse invested capital. Owner return runs through profit after costs, not through volume as a paycheck. Sales help create the chance; profit is the reimbursement channel.

So the statement is False.

Promotional bundles — multi-buy offers, package deals — are a familiar lever to stimulate higher sales volume quickly. They trade a sharper deal for a near-term lift in units moved. The statement describes that tool accurately.

So the statement is True.

title: Cost Coverage Misunderstandings
context: Analyze sales volume increases that strengthen cash inflows before profit is calculated. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profit reinvestment is prohibited when a firm pursues USP objectives.
Sales revenue flows from customers purchasing the product in the market.
There are no limitations on the link between higher sales and higher profit.
A marketing plan without sales targets would omit a core objective category.
Profitability is achieved when market share reaches fifty percent regardless of costs.
tactical_explanations:
USP work and profit reinvestment are compatible. A firm can plough earnings into better differentiation — packaging, service, formulation — rather than treating uniqueness goals as a ban on retention. Prohibiting reinvestment whenever a USP is pursued invents a false conflict.

Building a USP often needs money — better formulation, service, packaging — and retained profit is a natural source. Forbidding reinvestment whenever uniqueness is pursued would starve the very differentiation you claim to want.

So the statement is False.

Sales revenue comes from customers purchasing the product in the market. That purchase flow is the source of the money, not press mentions or internal transfer tricks. The statement's plain definition matches how the overview treats sales revenue.

So the statement is True.

There are limitations on the sales-profit link: discounts, rising costs, and mix shifts can break a simple "more sales, more profit" story. Claiming there are no limitations contradicts the chapter's careful wording. Volume helps; it does not guarantee.

So the statement is False.

A marketing plan that omits sales targets leaves out a core objective category. Satisfaction, share, and USP aims still need the volume/revenue layer. Skipping sales targets is an incomplete plan in the overview's terms.

So the statement is True.

Fifty percent share with uncontrolled costs does not equal profitability. Share is relative sales weight; profit needs revenue above costs. A dominant slice can still lose money. The "share percentage equals profit" shortcut is false.

Walk a firm that bought share with heavy discounting: the chart looks impressive while margins vanish. Profitability still demands cost and price discipline beside any share trophy.

Half the market with a broken cost base is still a loss-making half. Share trophies do not print profit certificates. Cost and price discipline remain required no matter what percentage you hold.

So the statement is False.

title: Reinvestment Objective Errors
context: Review limitations on the sales-profit link when discounting or costs offset volume gains. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Volume sold through online channels counts toward overall sales objectives.
Sales growth from loyal repeat customers is a sustainable volume source.
Production must be aligned with sales objectives to avoid unmet demand or excess stock.
A temporary sales spike from a campaign still counts toward period volume objectives.
Sales cover variable and fixed production costs when revenue is sufficient.
tactical_explanations:
Online channel volume counts toward overall sales objectives when that channel is part of how the firm sells. Clicks that become paid orders are sales, not a separate universe. Including digital volume in the total is normal.

So the statement is True.

Loyal repeat buyers are a sustainable source of sales growth because they return without being fully re-acquired each time. Volume built on that base tends to last longer than one-shot promo hunters. The statement flags that durability correctly.

Repeat buyers lower the perpetual reacquisition grind. Volume from that loyalty base tends to survive after the promo lights go off. Sustainability is why loyalty-fed growth is prized in sales objectives.

So the statement is True.

Production has to line up with sales objectives: underproduce and you miss demand; overproduce and you drown in stock. Alignment between what you make and what you aim to sell is practical planning, not optional perfectionism.

So the statement is True.

A campaign spike still counts toward the period's volume objective even if it is temporary. Period totals add the spike and the quieter weeks together. Temporary does not mean "does not count"; it means the shape of the month was uneven.

Managers reviewing a quarter that included a flash sale still credit those units to the sales target for that window. The spike is real volume in the period, even if sustainability needs a separate conversation afterward.

Period totals do not throw away the flash-sale week. Those units happened inside the window, so they count toward the period's volume objective even if next month needs a steadier mix. Temporary shape, real credit.

So the statement is True.

When revenue is large enough, sales cover both variable and fixed production costs — the materials that move with each unit and the overhead that sits there anyway. Sufficient revenue is what makes that dual coverage possible.

So the statement is True.

title: Repeat Purchase Denials
context: Analyze interrelated marketing objectives that reinforce one another across the customer lifecycle. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profits are unimportant because owners require no return on invested money.
A discounting strategy that maximises unit sales always maximises profit simultaneously.
Profitability objectives conflict with customer satisfaction and cannot coexist.
Marketing staff may compare actual sales to targeted sales each month.
Retained earnings from profit cannot finance marketing campaigns.
tactical_explanations:
Profits matter precisely because owners expect a return on money they invested. Calling profits unimportant because "owners need nothing" invents owners who are not investors. The chapter's reimbursement reason makes profit central, not optional decoration.

Investors who need no return are not the owners the chapter has in mind. Profit's importance is tied to reimbursing invested money. Calling profits unimportant on that false premise collapses the reason they are listed.

So the statement is False.

Maximise unit sales with deep discounts and you can destroy margin — more units, less profit. Volume maximisation and profit maximisation are not automatic twins. The "always simultaneously" claim fails whenever price cuts outrun cost savings.

So the statement is False.

Profitability and customer satisfaction can coexist: satisfied buyers support repeat sales that feed profitable revenue. Treating them as permanent enemies forces a false choice. Good firms pursue both in one objective set.

So the statement is False.

Comparing actual sales to targeted sales each month is ordinary marketing control. The variance tells staff whether campaigns and offers are landing. That comparison habit is how sales objectives stay measurable rather than aspirational posters.

So the statement is True.

Retained earnings from profit can finance marketing campaigns — brand work, launches, content — without always tapping new outside funds. Saying retained profit cannot fund marketing denies a standard internal-finance path.

If plough-back could not pay for campaigns, every promotion would need fresh borrowing or new equity. The overview treats retained profit as usable internal finance for such initiatives.

Next season's campaign can be funded from this year's retained surplus. Internal finance from profit is a standard path into marketing spend. "Cannot finance" denies a tool managers actually use.

So the statement is False.

title: Promotion-Only Differentiation
context: Review loyalty as an outcome when satisfaction leads customers to buy the product again. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Higher sales figures never contribute to profit under any market condition.
Increasing sales in export markets can be a marketing objective for growth.
Sales volume objectives may be adjusted after market analysis reveals demand limits.
Profit is recorded before sales revenue is earned from customers.
A price reduction might raise unit sales while affecting revenue per unit.
tactical_explanations:
Higher sales often contribute to profit when margins hold; saying they never contribute under any condition is an absolute the chapter rejects. The usual link is positive, with limitations — not a permanent ban on sales helping profit.

Under ordinary margins, more sales put more revenue into the profit calculation. "Never… under any market condition" denies the usual case the chapter starts from before it lists limitations. Absolute never is the error.

So the statement is False.

Growing sales in export markets is a legitimate marketing objective for firms seeking growth beyond the home field. Crossing a border does not remove volume from the objective set; it adds a growth arena.

So the statement is True.

After market analysis shows demand limits, sales volume objectives may be revised downward or reshaped. Targets should fit what the market can bear. Adjustment after analysis is disciplined planning, not weakness.

So the statement is True.

Profit is calculated after sales revenue is earned and costs are deducted — not before customers pay. Recording "profit" with no sales yet is accounting fiction relative to the trading story. Revenue comes first in that sequence.

Walk the timeline: offer → purchase → revenue → cost coverage → then surplus. Flipping profit ahead of sales breaks the order the overview uses when it links the two.

You cannot book trading profit before customers have paid. The sequence is purchase → revenue → costs → surplus. Parking profit ahead of sales revenue reverses that order.

So the statement is False.

A price cut can lift unit sales while shrinking revenue per unit — more bags sold, less euro per bag. Both effects can appear together. Managers have to watch volume and the revenue arithmetic, not only the unit count.

So the statement is True.

title: Share Maintenance Denials
context: Analyze unique selling propositions that position a product as better than the rest in buyers' minds. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Marketing success is judged only by share gains with no regard to profit.
Profit reinvestment means paying all revenue to suppliers immediately.
Profitability requires sales to fall so that costs can be eliminated.
Owners' invested money is reimbursed through promotional reach metrics.
Sales are important because they provide the funds to cover production costs and profit.
tactical_explanations:
Judging marketing success only by share gains while ignoring profit is a distorted scoreboard. Share can be bought with discounts that erase surplus. Relative standing matters, but the overview still keeps profitability in the objective set beside it.

So the statement is False.

Profit reinvestment means keeping earnings in the firm for future use — capacity, brand, products — not handing every euro of revenue straight to suppliers the day it arrives. Paying suppliers is cost settlement; reinvestment is surplus retained. The statement confuses the two cash stories.

Paying suppliers clears invoices; reinvesting profit keeps surplus for tomorrow's capacity or brand. Collapsing those into "pay all revenue to suppliers immediately" misnames reinvestment as cost settlement.

So the statement is False.

Profitability does not require sales to fall so costs can be "eliminated." Cutting volume to chase zero cost is not the profit path the chapter describes. Profit usually needs adequate sales revenue above costs, not a shrinkage fantasy.

So the statement is False.

Owners' invested money is reimbursed through profits, not through promotional reach metrics like impressions or click counts. Reach can support sales that later fund profit, but the reimbursement itself is a profit outcome. Equating owner return with ad-reach dashboards mislabels the objective.

If that were true, a viral campaign with empty tills would "reimburse" owners.

Impressions and reach can support future sales, but they are not the reimbursement of owners' capital. That reimbursement is a profit outcome. Confusing ad dashboards with owner return mislabels the objective.

So the statement is False.

Sales are important because they provide the funds that cover production costs and, when margins allow, contribute to profit. That dual commercial job — cost cover plus path to surplus — is why sales sit among marketing objectives rather than as optional noise.

So the statement is True.

title: Volume Profit Assumptions
context: Review market share as a relative measure rather than an absolute sales total alone. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Volume targets at retail level roll up to manufacturer sales objectives.
A USP guarantees profit without regard to sales volume or costs.
A business may prioritise sales growth when entering a new customer segment.
Profitability objectives apply only when the firm has no competitors.
Retained profit must be distributed entirely to creditors each year.
tactical_explanations:
Retail-level volume targets roll upward into the manufacturer's sales picture when the brand sells through stores. What leaves the shelf feeds what the maker counts as sales in that channel system. Roll-up from retail targets to manufacturer objectives is normal chain thinking.

When retail doors carry the brand, store volume targets feed what the manufacturer needs to hit. The chain rolls numbers upward. Separating retail targets from maker sales objectives as if they never meet ignores how channel systems work.

So the statement is True.

A USP does not guarantee profit regardless of sales volume or costs. Uniqueness can support preference and pricing, but without enough sales or with runaway costs, profit still fails. Treating USP as an automatic profit machine skips the arithmetic.

So the statement is False.

Entering a new customer segment often comes with a deliberate sales-growth priority — win early volume, learn the segment, build presence. Prioritising growth there is a recognised marketing choice during entry, not a rule violation.

So the statement is True.

Profitability objectives apply whether the firm faces many rivals or few. Competition may change how hard profit is to earn, but it does not switch the profit objective off. "Only when there are no competitors" invents a monopoly-only rule the chapter does not teach.

Walk a crowded specialty category: margins are contested, yet managers still set profit aims beside share and sales. Rival density changes tactics; it does not erase profitability from the objective list.

Crowded markets still need profit aims. Rival count changes how hard surplus is to earn; it does not delete profitability from the objective list. Monopoly-only profit rules are invented, not taught.

So the statement is False.

Retained profit need not be handed entirely to creditors each year. Retention means keeping earnings in the business; mandatory full payout to creditors confuses debt service with the retained-earnings concept. Some profit may service obligations; the rest can stay invested.

So the statement is False.

title: Objective Hierarchy Mistakes
context: Analyze maintaining sales as essential for ongoing revenue to fund business activity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Limitations on the sales-profit link mean higher sales always lower profit.
Sales performance relative to plan indicates marketing effectiveness.
Revenue objectives are closely tied to sales volume and selling price.
Profitability is unrelated to marketing because marketing generates only costs.
Maintaining sales during an economic downturn can be a demanding marketing objective.
tactical_explanations:
Limitations on the sales-profit link mean higher sales do not automatically raise profit — not that higher sales always lower it. The careful reading is "not guaranteed upward," not "always downward." Flipping the limitation into permanent damage misstates the warning.

The limitation says "not automatically more profit," not "always less profit." Misreading the warning as permanent damage from every sales increase flips a caution into a false law.

So the statement is False.

Sales against plan is a standard read on marketing effectiveness: did the campaigns, offers, and coverage move volume as intended? Performance relative to the target is evidence, not decoration. The statement places that indicator correctly.

So the statement is True.

Revenue objectives lean on both sales volume and selling price — units times price shape the euro total. Ignore either lever and the revenue story is incomplete. The tight tie the statement names is how managers build revenue aims from commercial ingredients.

So the statement is True.

Marketing generates costs, yes, but it also aims to generate sales that fund surplus. Calling profitability unrelated because marketing "only generates costs" ignores the revenue side of the marketing job. Profit and marketing remain linked through that sales path.

If marketing were pure cost with no commercial purpose, firms would not fund it. The overview treats marketing objectives as contributing toward profitable outcomes, not as a permanent cost sink sealed off from profit talk.

Marketing spends money to win sales that can create surplus. Treating it as a pure cost centre with no link to profitability ignores why firms fund marketing at all. The unrelatedness claim severs that bridge.

So the statement is False.

Holding sales steady in a downturn can be one of the hardest marketing objectives — demand softens, rivals discount, buyers delay. Maintenance under pressure is still a real goal, and often a demanding one. The statement recognises that difficulty correctly.

So the statement is True.

title: Customer Needs Neglect
context: Review profitability enabling owners to be reimbursed and the firm to retain funds internally. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Sales from repeat purchases reduce dependence on costly new customer acquisition.
A marketing objective to double sales implies a substantial volume increase target.
Sales growth supports the broader aim of making a profit after covering costs.
Trade promotions to retailers may aim to lift sell-through sales volume.
A firm with high customer satisfaction cannot pursue profitability objectives.
tactical_explanations:
Repeat purchases from existing customers reduce the need to keep buying expensive new acquisition every week. Loyalty volume is cheaper to keep than cold traffic is to win. That dependence shift is why repeats matter for efficient sales growth.

So the statement is True.

Doubling sales is a substantial volume-increase target by definition — twice the units or revenue of the base. Naming that objective commits the firm to a large commercial step, not a cosmetic tweak. The implication the statement draws is fair.

So the statement is True.

Sales growth supports the broader aim of making a profit after costs are covered: more revenue material for the surplus calculation, provided margins hold. Growth is not identical to profit, but it feeds the path the overview describes.

So the statement is True.

Trade promotions aimed at retailers — allowances, display deals, temporary discounts — often exist to lift sell-through volume. The manufacturer wants product moving off the retailer's shelf into baskets. That sales-volume aim is why such promotions appear in the plan.

Retailer allowances and display deals exist to move product into baskets. Sell-through volume is the commercial point of those trade promotions. Aiming them at lift is ordinary practice, not a side curiosity.

So the statement is True.

High satisfaction does not bar profitability objectives. Satisfied customers often help profit through repeats and lower churn. Claiming a firm with strong satisfaction "cannot" pursue profit invents a ban that contradicts interrelated objectives.

Note: satisfaction and profit reinforce each other when repeats and willingness to pay stay healthy — they are not mutually exclusive switches.

Satisfied buyers often help profit through repeats. High satisfaction is a reason to keep profit objectives, not a ban on them. Mutual exclusion invents a conflict the interrelated set does not require.

So the statement is False.

title: Perceived Uniqueness Denials
context: Analyze how businesses set marketing objectives after analysing the markets they wish to operate in. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Sales monitoring by region helps allocate marketing resources effectively.
Volume sold is a direct measure of progress on sales-related marketing objectives.
Sales revenue must be earned before profit can be distributed or retained.
A firm may accept lower margin temporarily to achieve a sales volume milestone.
Marketing objectives on sales recognise that businesses need revenues to operate.
tactical_explanations:
Watching sales by region shows where demand is strong or weak so managers can aim budget, stock, and effort where they work. Regional monitoring is a resource-allocation tool, not paperwork for its own sake. The statement captures that planning use.

So the statement is True.

Volume sold is a direct progress measure on sales-related marketing objectives. If the aim was units or revenue, the realised volume says whether you are on track. It is the obvious yardstick for those aims.

So the statement is True.

Sales revenue has to be earned before profit can be distributed to owners or retained in the firm. Without the revenue event, there is no surplus to split or plough back. The sequence — earn, then allocate — is the statement's point.

So the statement is True.

Firms sometimes accept a thinner margin for a stretch to hit a sales volume milestone — launch scale, channel entry, or a share foothold. Temporary margin sacrifice for volume is a recognised trade-off, not automatic mismanagement, when it is chosen deliberately.

Walk a launch that prices sharp to fill distribution: unit margin dips while volume clears the milestone. Managers still watch the clock on that trade-off; the statement only says the acceptance can happen, which it can.

Launch milestones sometimes need sharp prices for a stretch. Accepting thinner margin temporarily to clear a volume gate is a deliberate trade-off when timed and watched — not proof that margin never matters.

So the statement is True.

Sales objectives recognise that businesses need revenues to operate — to pay for production, keep doors open, and fund the rest of the plan. That need is why maintaining or growing sales sits in the marketing objective set rather than as an afterthought.

Without revenues, operations stall. Sales objectives exist because that revenue need is real. Recognising the need is why sales stay in the marketing objective vocabulary.

So the statement is True.

title: Competitiveness Indicator Traps
context: Review the role of customer satisfaction as a marketing objective linked to repeat purchase and loyalty. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profit reinvestment is the same as issuing new share capital to investors.
Higher sales from satisfied loyal customers illustrate interrelated marketing objectives.
Sales targets for a new store opening reflect geographic expansion objectives.
Volume growth without cost control may fail to improve profitability.
Sales covering production costs is sufficient for profit with no margin required.
tactical_explanations:
Profit reinvestment is keeping earned surplus inside the firm; issuing new share capital is raising fresh money from investors. They are different finance moves. Equating plough-back with a new share issue collapses internal earnings into external equity.

So the statement is False.

Higher sales from satisfied loyal customers show how objectives interrelate: satisfaction feeds loyalty, loyalty feeds volume. One chart movement can be the joint result of several aims working together. The illustration the statement points to is classic overview logic.

So the statement is True.

Sales targets for a new store opening express geographic expansion in volume language — what that site should sell as it comes online. Expansion objectives and sales targets meet in that opening plan. The statement links them correctly.

So the statement is True.

Volume growth without cost control can leave profitability flat or worse. More units with wasteful overtime, spoil, or freight can erase the gain. Growth is not a profit spell unless costs are kept in view.

A bakery that doubles weekend output but burns ingredients and temp labour may see busy tills and a weaker surplus. The statement's warning about cost control is the limitation side of the sales-profit link.

Busy volume with uncontrolled overtime, waste, or freight can leave the surplus untouched or worse. Cost control is the companion that turns growth into profit improvement. Without it, growth is incomplete.

So the statement is True.

Covering production costs is necessary for profit but not sufficient by itself if you mean a comfortable surplus — managers still care about margin above mere break-even. Saying cost coverage alone equals profit with "no margin required" undersells what profitability objectives aim for.

Break-even coverage is the floor; profitability objectives usually aim above it for a meaningful margin. Calling mere cost cover "sufficient… with no margin required" undersells what profit aims ask for.

So the statement is False.

title: Revenue Flow Assertions
context: Analyze how a unique selling proposition supports product differentiation and attracts loyal customers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profitability is a marketing objective because profits reimburse owners for invested money.
Profits can be retained and reinvested in the business for future growth.
Usually the higher the sales figures are, the more profit a business will make, with certain limitations.
Profitability objectives sit alongside satisfaction, differentiation, share, and sales goals.
Marketing success ultimately contributes to profit when revenues exceed relevant costs.
tactical_explanations:
Profitability is a marketing objective because profits reimburse owners for money they put into the firm. That return-on-invested-capital reason is why profit sits in the objective set, not only in the finance department's private language.

So the statement is True.

Profits can be kept in the business and reinvested for future growth — new capacity, better offers, stronger brand. Plough-back is a strategic use of earnings, not a forbidden leftover. The statement names that retention path correctly.

So the statement is True.

Usually higher sales figures mean more profit — more revenue to work with — but certain limitations apply: costs, discounts, and mix can break the simple upward story. The statement's "usually… with certain limitations" wording matches the chapter's careful link.

Read the sentence as the chapter writes it: usually upward, with limitations when costs or discounts intervene. That balanced claim is stronger teaching than either naive optimism or permanent pessimism.

So the statement is True.

Profitability sits alongside satisfaction, differentiation, share, and sales in the marketing objectives overview. It is one seat at the table, not a replacement for the others and not an exile from the list. Parallel placement is the design.

Managers therefore write profit aims next to volume and share rather than treating profit as a topic that only appears after marketing leaves the room. The statement's "alongside" reading is the right architecture.

Satisfaction, USP, share, sales, and profit share one planning table. Profitability is not a late guest and not a replacement for the others. Alongside means parallel membership in the objective set.

So the statement is True.

Marketing success ultimately helps profit when the sales it generates exceed the relevant costs those activities and the product carry. Revenue above cost is the bridge from marketing work to surplus. The statement closes that loop in the overview's terms.

So the statement is True.

title: Owner Return Misconceptions
context: Review why gaining and maintaining market share indicates a firm's relative competitiveness. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profitability is measured by customer satisfaction scores rather than financial surplus.
Owners expect profits as compensation for the capital they invested in the firm.
Retained profit can finance new equipment without raising external finance.
A profitability target may be expressed as a margin percentage on sales.
Higher sales support profitability when unit margins and costs remain favourable.
tactical_explanations:
Profitability is a financial surplus idea — revenue above costs — not a customer satisfaction score. Satisfaction can support profitable sales, but the measure of profitability is not the survey mean. Swapping the scorecard confuses related objectives.

Survey scores track experience; profit tracks surplus. Related, yes — identical measures, no. Using satisfaction as the profitability meter confuses two different objective languages.

So the statement is False.

Owners expect profits as compensation for capital they invested. That expectation is why profitability objectives matter in the marketing overview's story about returns. The statement restates the reimbursement logic cleanly.

So the statement is True.

Retained profit can pay for new equipment without immediately raising a bank loan or new equity. Internal surplus is a funding source for assets that support future operations. Financing kit from plough-back is exactly that use case.

So the statement is True.

A profitability target often appears as a margin percentage on sales — gross margin, operating margin, and similar ratios. Expressing the aim that way ties surplus to the sales base. Percentage-on-sales language is normal for profit objectives.

So the statement is True.

Higher sales support profitability when unit margins stay healthy and costs do not run away. Under those favourable conditions, more volume feeds more surplus. The conditional wording is doing real work — support is not unconditional.

If margins collapse while volume rises, the support can vanish. The statement keeps the favourable-margin caveat in view, which is how the chapter wants the sales-profit link read.

Favourable unit margins and contained costs are the conditions under which higher sales feed profit. Drop either condition and the support can fail. The caveat is doing real analytical work.

So the statement is True.

title: Satisfaction Sales Interlink
context: Analyze the importance of maintaining or increasing sales to cover production costs and earn profit. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profit objectives acknowledge that sales alone do not guarantee profit in every case.
Marketing campaigns are assessed partly on whether they improve profitable sales.
Reinvestment of profit supports long-term marketing and production capacity.
Profitability is important because it sustains the business for owners and reinvestment.
Higher sales always eliminate the need to reinvest profit in the business.
tactical_explanations:
Profit objectives exist partly because sales alone do not guarantee profit in every case — costs and prices can spoil the ending. Acknowledging that gap is why profit is tracked as its own aim beside volume. The statement's humility about sales is correct.

Volume can disappoint on surplus when costs or prices misbehave. Profit objectives exist to catch those cases rather than assume every sales win is a profit win. Acknowledgement of the gap is the point.

So the statement is True.

Campaigns are judged partly on whether they improve profitable sales, not only on noise or reach. A lift in unprofitable volume can fail the commercial test. Bringing profitable sales into the assessment keeps marketing tied to surplus, not vanity metrics.

So the statement is True.

Reinvesting profit builds long-term marketing and production capacity — better lines, more output, stronger brand tools. Plough-back is forward-looking fuel, not a leftover afterthought. The statement places reinvestment in that capacity role.

So the statement is True.

Profitability sustains the business for owners who need returns and for the firm that needs funds to reinvest. Without surplus over time, both reimbursement and internal growth starve. Importance follows from that dual sustainment job.

Walk a firm that never clears a durable surplus: owners lose patience and capacity plans stall. The overview treats profitability as the objective that keeps that dual engine running.

Owners need returns; the firm needs fuel to reinvest. Profitability is what keeps both possible over time. Sustaining that dual engine is why the objective earns its importance.

So the statement is True.

Higher sales never automatically eliminate the need to reinvest profit. Growth often increases the need for capacity, stock, and brand investment. Volume success is a reason to plan reinvestment carefully, not a licence to skip plough-back forever.

So the statement is False.

title: USP Loyalty Connection
context: Review profitability as a marketing objective and its link to reimbursing owners and reinvestment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A firm may reject unprofitable volume that fails margin thresholds.
Profit objectives are met when advertising spending equals total revenue.
Owners receive reimbursement only through wages, never through profit.
Cost increases can offset sales growth and limit profit improvement.
Profit retained in the business reduces dependence on external borrowing for expansion.
tactical_explanations:
Firms may refuse volume that fails margin thresholds — orders that would clear the warehouse but wreck profitability. Rejecting unprofitable volume is disciplined profit management, not a fear of sales. The statement allows that selective "no."

So the statement is True.

Profit objectives are not met merely because advertising spend equals total revenue. That equality could mean all revenue was spent on ads with nothing left for product costs or surplus. Matching ad spend to revenue is not a profit definition.

So the statement is False.

Owners can be reimbursed through profit, not only through wages for labour they happen to supply. Capital return and wage income are different channels. Saying owners receive reimbursement "only through wages, never through profit" erases the capital-return story.

Wages pay for labour time; profit returns capital. Owners who invested money are reimbursed through surplus, not only through a paycheck if they also work. "Only wages, never profit" erases capital return.

So the statement is False.

Cost increases can cancel sales growth's help on profit — more revenue, but even more expense. The offset is a classic limitation on the sales-profit link. Growth then fails to improve the surplus even though the top line moved.

Picture a campaign that lifts bookings while energy, staffing, and ingredient costs jump faster: sales look better, profit does not. The statement's offset warning is the limitation paragraph in action.

Sales can rise while input costs rise faster — energy, materials, staffing — and the surplus stalls. Offsetting cost growth is a textbook limitation on reading volume as automatic profit improvement.

So the statement is True.

Keeping profit in the business reduces how much expansion must lean on external borrowing. Internal funds can pay for growth steps that would otherwise need a loan. Retention as a substitute for some outside finance is the practical advantage named here.

So the statement is True.

title: Relative Importance Measures
context: Analyze how customer satisfaction interrelates with other marketing objectives such as sales and loyalty. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Marketing objectives include profitability because owners need returns on investment.
Discounting that raises sales volume may reduce profitability per unit sold.
Profit measurement follows revenue from sales minus the costs of production and marketing.
A profitability review examines whether marketing spend generated adequate returns.
Profitability and market share move in opposite directions in every case.
tactical_explanations:
Marketing objectives include profitability because owners need returns on what they invested. That owner-return reason pulls profit into the marketing objective conversation rather than leaving it as a pure finance afterthought.

So the statement is True.

Discounting can raise unit sales while cutting profit per unit — more baskets, thinner margin on each. Volume and unit profitability can move in opposite directions under a heavy discount. The statement flags that tension correctly.

So the statement is True.

Profit is measured from sales revenue minus production and marketing costs. That subtraction is the basic shape of the surplus calculation. The statement's "follows revenue… minus costs" wording matches how managers read profit against marketing activity.

So the statement is True.

A profitability review asks whether marketing spend produced adequate returns — did the campaign euros come back as enough surplus? That return check is how profit objectives discipline marketing budgets rather than treating spend as unlimited.

Managers comparing campaign cost to contribution or margin lift are doing exactly that review. The statement places profitability assessment on marketing's results, which is where the overview wants it.

Did the campaign euros come back as enough contribution or margin? That question is a profitability review of marketing spend. Adequate returns are how profit objectives discipline the budget.

So the statement is True.

Profitability and market share do not move in opposite directions in every case. They can rise together, fall together, or diverge depending on pricing and costs. "Always opposite" is a false universal. Relative standing and surplus are related but not locked in permanent conflict.

Share and profit can climb together under premium pricing, or diverge under discount wars. Opposite-every-time is a false law. Direction depends on how the slice was won.

So the statement is False.

title: Production Cost Coverage
context: Review how product differentiation can rest on product characteristics or on promotion and customer perception. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Satisfied loyal customers who buy repeatedly can improve lifetime profitability.
Profit reinvestment may fund brand-building that supports future differentiation.
Higher sales figures usually mean more profit, though limitations such as rising costs apply.
Profitability objectives encourage attention to cost coverage, not only gross revenue.
Owners may withdraw part of profit as income while retaining the rest in the business.
tactical_explanations:
Satisfied loyal customers who buy again improve lifetime profitability: more purchases over time, lower repeated acquisition cost, steadier revenue. The lifetime lens is why satisfaction and loyalty matter for profit, not only for soft brand feelings.

So the statement is True.

Reinvesting profit can fund brand-building that supports future differentiation — identity, packaging, story, proof. Plough-back into brand is how today's surplus becomes tomorrow's uniqueness. The funding link the statement names is real strategy.

So the statement is True.

Higher sales figures usually mean more profit, though rising costs and other limitations can break the pattern. The "usually… though limitations apply" shape is the chapter's own careful claim. Reading it that way keeps both the tendency and the caveat.

Hold the "usually" and the "limitations" in one breath. That is the chapter's voice on sales and profit — tendency with exceptions — not a blank cheque and not a permanent denial.

So the statement is True.

Profitability objectives push attention onto cost coverage, not only onto gross revenue headlines. A big top line with uncovered costs fails the profit aim. The discipline is surplus after costs, which is why coverage sits inside profit thinking.

Walk a firm celebrating record sales while overtime and waste erase the margin: revenue vanity without coverage focus misses the profitability objective. The statement steers managers back to that coverage requirement.

Gross revenue headlines without coverage discipline miss what profitability asks. Attention to whether sales clear costs is the objective doing its job. Coverage focus is not optional decoration.

So the statement is True.

Owners may take part of profit as income and leave the rest in the business. Withdrawal and retention can split the same surplus. Both uses appear in the overview's story about what profit is for.

So the statement is True.

title: Profit Limitation Awareness
context: Analyze why building a brand supports the creation of a unique selling proposition. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A marketing plan should consider whether sales targets are profit-compatible.
Profit from one product line can subsidise marketing investment in another line.
Profitability is linked to sales because sales provide the revenue base for profit calculation.
Retained earnings from profit strengthen the firm's internal finance for marketing.
A firm pursuing share at the expense of margin may temporarily reduce profitability.
tactical_explanations:
A marketing plan should ask whether sales targets are compatible with profit — volume that only works via destructive discounting may fail the profit side. Checking profit-compatibility keeps the objective set coherent rather than writing conflicting numbers.

A sales target that only works via margin-killing discounts may fail the profit side of the plan. Checking compatibility up front keeps the objective set from fighting itself later.

So the statement is True.

Profit from a strong line can subsidise marketing investment in another line still being built. Cross-subsidy inside the firm is a recognised use of surplus. One product's earnings funding another's push is ordinary portfolio practice.

So the statement is True.

Profitability links to sales because sales provide the revenue base entering the profit calculation. No sales revenue, no ordinary trading profit. The base-layer link is why the two objectives are discussed together.

So the statement is True.

Retained earnings from profit strengthen internal finance available for marketing — campaigns, launches, research — without always opening an external tap. Stronger internal funds make marketing initiatives easier to resource from inside.

A firm that ploughs surplus into next season's brand push is using retained profit as marketing finance. The statement's strengthening claim matches that internal-funding path.

Campaigns and launches can draw on retained earnings instead of waiting for a loan committee. Stronger internal finance from profit makes marketing initiatives easier to start from inside.

So the statement is True.

Chasing share with heavy margin sacrifice can temporarily reduce profitability even if the slice grows. Share gains and profit dips can coexist for a stretch. The trade-off is real; the statement names it without pretending share always pays immediately.

So the statement is True.

title: Integrated Marketing Objective Review
context: Review how market share reflects a business position relative to competitors in the same market. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profit objectives motivate efficient use of marketing budgets.
Limitations on the sales-profit link include unfavourable changes in unit costs.
Profitability allows owners to be compensated while the firm retains funds for growth.
Marketing staff may track gross profit by product to align with profitability objectives.
A USP supporting premium pricing can improve profitability if costs are controlled.
tactical_explanations:
Profit objectives motivate careful use of marketing budgets: spend should earn its keep in commercial returns, not vanish into unmeasured activity. Efficiency pressure comes from caring about surplus, not only about noise. The motivational link is practical discipline.

When surplus matters, wasteful spend looks expensive. Profit objectives push marketers to ask whether budget lines earn commercial returns. Efficiency is motivated by caring about that surplus.

So the statement is True.

Unfavourable unit-cost changes are a listed limitation on the sales-profit link. Sell more while unit costs jump and the surplus may stall. The limitation language exists for exactly those cost surprises beside volume gains.

So the statement is True.

Profitability lets owners be compensated and lets the firm keep funds for growth at the same time — split the surplus between withdrawal and retention. Both jobs sit on the profit outcome. The dual use is why profit objectives matter broadly.

So the statement is True.

Marketing staff often track gross profit by product to stay aligned with profitability objectives — which lines earn, which only look busy. Product-level profit tracking turns the profit aim into day-to-day steering, not a year-end surprise.

Walk a category review where one SKU's gross profit is thin despite strong units: marketers may reshape promotion or price rather than keep pouring spend into empty calories. That tracking habit is the statement's point.

Product-level gross profit charts show which lines deserve push and which only look busy. Tracking that way aligns daily marketing choices with profitability objectives rather than waiting for a year-end shock.

So the statement is True.

A USP that supports premium pricing can improve profitability when costs stay controlled — higher price, healthy margin. Uniqueness helps the price story; cost control keeps the surplus. Both conditions matter for the profit lift.

So the statement is True.

title: Closing Objective Distinctions
context: Analyze the relationship between higher sales figures and profitability within stated limitations. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profit reinvestment in production capacity can support future sales growth.
Profitability is a stated marketing objective in the textbook marketing overview.
Sales must cover production costs before any profit can be recorded.
Owners reinvest profit when they expect future returns from expanded operations.
A decline in profitability despite stable sales may reflect higher input costs.
tactical_explanations:
Reinvesting profit into production capacity — more ovens, more lines, more rooms — can support future sales growth by making higher volume physically possible. Today's surplus becomes tomorrow's throughput. The capacity bridge is a standard reinvestment rationale.

More capacity from reinvested profit can unlock sales the old plant could not serve. Future volume often needs today's surplus turned into ovens, lines, or rooms. That bridge is why capacity plough-back is strategic.

So the statement is True.

Profitability appears as a stated marketing objective in the textbook marketing overview alongside satisfaction, differentiation, share, and sales. It is on the list, not smuggled in from another chapter. The statement's "stated… in the overview" claim holds.

So the statement is True.

Sales must cover production costs before any profit can be recorded in the ordinary trading sense. Below that coverage line there is loss, not surplus. The sequencing the statement gives is the cost-coverage prerequisite.

So the statement is True.

Owners reinvest profit when they expect future returns from expanded operations — a bigger footprint, a stronger brand, more capacity earning later. Expectation of future return is the economic reason to plough back rather than withdraw everything now.

If no future return were expected, retention would look pointless. The overview's reinvestment story assumes that forward-looking payoff motive, which the statement names.

Owners leave money in when they expect expanded operations to pay them back later. Reinvestment is a bet on future returns, not a ritual. That expectation motive is the economic reason to retain.

So the statement is True.

Stable sales with falling profitability often point to higher input costs — materials, energy, labour — squeezing the margin while volume holds. The diagnostic the statement offers is a common reading of that pattern.

So the statement is True.

title: Final Marketing Goals Assessment
context: Review why dissatisfied customers are unlikely to buy a product again. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profit targets may be set annually alongside sales and share objectives.
Marketing that attracts profitable customer segments supports profitability objectives.
Retained profit is internally generated finance for marketing initiatives.
The relationship between sales and profit is positive in general but not without exceptions.
Profitability objectives remind managers that revenue growth must exceed cost growth.
tactical_explanations:
Profit targets may be set annually next to sales and share objectives on the same planning sheet. Parallel annual targets keep the objective set visible together. Co-setting them is ordinary marketing planning rhythm.

So the statement is True.

Attracting customer segments that are profitable supports profitability objectives — not every buyer is equal on margin. Marketing that aims at valuable segments is doing profit work, not only headcount work. Segment quality matters for the surplus aim.

Chasing every possible buyer can fill volume with thin-margin pain. Aiming marketing at segments that clear profit tests supports the profitability objective directly. Segment quality is part of the surplus story.

So the statement is True.

Retained profit is internally generated finance for marketing initiatives — money the firm earned and kept, then spent on campaigns or development. That internal character is what distinguishes plough-back from new loans or new equity.

So the statement is True.

The sales-profit relationship is positive in general — more sales tend to help — but not without exceptions when costs or prices intervene. General tendency plus exceptions is exactly how the chapter frames the link. Absolute guarantees are the mistake.

Managers who treat every volume uptick as automatic profit are ignoring the exception cases. The statement's balanced wording is the disciplined reading.

Exceptions appear when discounts deepen or costs spike. The general positive link survives as a tendency; the exceptions keep managers from treating volume as a profit spell. Both halves belong in the reading.

So the statement is True.

Profitability objectives remind managers that revenue growth must outpace cost growth for surplus to improve. Top-line motion alone is not enough if expenses sprint faster. The reminder function keeps cost discipline beside sales ambition.

So the statement is True.

title: Comprehensive Objective Assertions
context: Analyze how a unique selling proposition makes a product seem special, unique, or better than alternatives. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Retained profit cannot support production capacity expansion.
A profitability objective is fulfilled when the firm has the most employees.
A business may analyse contribution margin per unit to support profit objectives.
Marketing that raises sales with rising costs always increases profit.
Profitability is excluded when businesses analyse customer wishes and needs.
tactical_explanations:
Retained profit can support production capacity expansion — that is one of its standard jobs. Saying it cannot fund capacity growth denies the reinvestment path the overview describes. Plough-back into plant and throughput is allowed and common.

So the statement is False.

Having the most employees does not fulfil a profitability objective. Headcount is not surplus. A crowded payroll can even pressure costs. Profit aims are about financial results, not winning a staffing contest.

So the statement is False.

Contribution margin per unit — what each unit leaves after variable costs — is a practical analytic tool supporting profit objectives. Managers use it to see which sales help the surplus. Analysing contribution is aligned with caring about profit.

So the statement is True.

Raising sales while costs rise faster does not always increase profit; the net can fall. "Always increases profit" ignores the cost side. The joint movement of sales and costs decides the surplus, not sales alone.

Walk a promotion that doubles volume while freight and overtime more than eat the extra revenue: sales up, profit down. The statement's absolute "always" fails on that familiar pattern.

Rising costs can outrun rising sales and leave profit lower. "Always increases" refuses that possibility. Joint movement of revenue and cost decides the outcome — sales alone do not.

So the statement is False.

Profitability is not excluded when firms analyse customer wishes and needs. Needs analysis informs offers that can sell profitably; it does not exile profit from the conversation. Excluding profitability from needs work invents a silo the overview does not require.

Needs analysis shapes offers that can sell; profit still sits among the aims those offers serve. Excluding profitability from wishes-and-needs work builds a silo the overview does not demand.

So the statement is False.

title: Late-Stage USP and Share Cases
context: Review the marketing objective of maintaining sales volume to generate revenue. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profits reimburse owners and can be ploughed back into the business per the text.
Marketing objectives on profit recognise limitations when discounting erodes margins.
Higher sales volume increases the revenue pool from which profit is calculated after costs.
Profit retention funds improvements that may later support customer satisfaction.
Profits are important only for tax purposes and not for reinvestment.
tactical_explanations:
Profits reimburse owners and can be ploughed back into the business — both uses appear in the text's account of why profit matters. Compensation and reinvestment sit side by side. The statement's dual wording matches that textbook pairing.

So the statement is True.

Profit-focused marketing objectives recognise limitations such as discounting that erodes margins: volume may rise while surplus does not. Building that limitation into profit thinking stops naive "more sales always means more profit" planning.

So the statement is True.

Higher sales volume enlarges the revenue pool from which profit is calculated after costs. More units or more invoices mean a bigger starting pile before cost subtraction. The pool image is how volume feeds the profit calculation's first term.

So the statement is True.

Keeping profit in the firm can fund improvements — service, product, training — that later support customer satisfaction. Retention today can become a better experience tomorrow. The lag from plough-back to satisfaction is a real strategic chain.

A hotel that reinvests surplus into faster check-in and better bedding is using retained profit to lift later guest scores. The statement's "may later support" link is that delayed payoff, not an instant magic trick.

Better bedding, faster desks, trained staff — improvements funded from retained profit show up later in guest scores. The lag from plough-back to satisfaction is delayed, but it is a real strategic chain.

So the statement is True.

Profits matter for reinvestment and owner returns, not "only for tax purposes." Reducing profit's importance to tax paperwork erases the commercial reasons the chapter stresses. Tax may be a consequence; it is not the sole point of earning surplus.

Reinvestment and owner returns are the commercial reasons profit matters. Tax may follow from surplus; it is not the sole purpose of earning it. "Only for tax" shrinks the chapter's account to paperwork.

So the statement is False.

title: Terminal Profit and Sales Review
context: Analyze how retained profit from higher sales can be reinvested in the business. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profitability assessment includes whether marketing achieved cost-effective sales growth.
Owners' invested money is reimbursed through profits earned from successful operations.
A firm may delay profit growth while investing heavily in brand and USP development.
Profit reinvestment is a strategic use of earnings kept within the business.
Limitations on sales-driven profit include simultaneous increases in marketing expenditure.
tactical_explanations:
Profitability assessment asks whether marketing delivered cost-effective sales growth — volume that was worth what it cost to win. Effectiveness on that test is how profit objectives judge marketing results beyond raw activity counts.

So the statement is True.

Owners get reimbursed for invested money through profits earned when operations succeed. Successful trading creates the surplus that compensates capital. The statement's reimbursement path matches the overview's owner-return logic.

So the statement is True.

A firm may postpone profit growth while pouring spend into brand and USP development — investing now for differentiation later. Delayed profit growth during brand-building is a recognised strategic choice, not automatic failure of the profit idea.

So the statement is True.

Profit reinvestment is precisely the strategic use of earnings kept inside the business rather than fully withdrawn. Capacity, marketing, and product improvement are typical destinations. The definition the statement gives is the concept's core.

Managers choosing plough-back are making a strategic allocation of surplus. Calling that a strategic use of retained earnings is not rhetoric — it is how the overview frames the decision.

Choosing to keep earnings inside for capacity or brand is a strategic allocation of surplus. That is what profit reinvestment means in the overview — use of retained earnings, not a leftover accident.

So the statement is True.

Sales-driven profit faces limitations when marketing expenditure rises at the same time — the extra volume may be expensive to buy. Simultaneous spend increases can blunt or erase the surplus gain from higher sales. That limitation belongs in the reading.

Buy volume with a huge marketing bill and the surplus gain from higher sales can shrink or vanish. Simultaneous spend increases are a named limitation on reading sales-driven profit too simply.

So the statement is True.

title: Marketing Case 100
context: Review the interdependence of customer satisfaction, differentiation, market share, sales, and profitability objectives. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Profitability and sales objectives are interrelated but not identical measures.
Marketing performance should ultimately contribute to sustainable profitability.
Retained profit strengthens the balance sheet for future marketing campaigns.
Profit per unit may fall even when total sales volume rises if prices are cut sharply.
Marketing objectives exclude profitability whenever sales volume targets are set.
tactical_explanations:
Profitability and sales objectives are interrelated — sales feed the revenue that can become profit — but they are not identical measures. Volume can look fine while surplus fails, and vice versa in odd cost cases. Related yet distinct is the accurate pairing.

So the statement is True.

Marketing performance should ultimately help sustainable profitability: offers, campaigns, and relationships that support surplus over time, not only one noisy week. Sustainability keeps the profit aim from collapsing into short sugar rushes. The "ultimately contribute" claim matches that destination.

So the statement is True.

Retained profit strengthens the balance sheet for future marketing campaigns by leaving resources inside the firm. Stronger internal funds make it easier to resource the next push without immediate outside finance. Balance-sheet strength is a practical benefit of retention.

So the statement is True.

Sharp price cuts can lift total sales volume while profit per unit falls — more units, thinner margin each. Volume and unit profit diverge under aggressive discounting. The statement's "may fall even when total sales volume rises" pattern is the classic trade-off.

Walk a weekend promo that fills carts at a deep cut: unit count soars, contribution per unit shrinks, and managers must check whether total profit rose or fell. Per-unit profit weakness amid volume strength is exactly what the claim describes.

Deep cuts fill carts and thin the margin on each unit. Total volume can set records while profit per unit slides. Managers must check the total surplus, not celebrate units alone — that is the trade-off the claim describes.

So the statement is True.

Setting sales volume targets does not exclude profitability from the marketing objective set. Firms routinely write both on the same plan. "Exclude profitability whenever sales targets exist" invents a false either-or the overview rejects.

Note: sales and profit aims can tension under discounting, but coexistence in the objective list is normal — exclusion is the error.

Plans routinely carry sales targets and profit aims together. Volume goals do not eject profitability from the set. Either-or exclusion is the error; coexistence is the normal design.

So the statement is False.

title: Product Orientation Versus Market Orientation
context: Review how product-oriented and market-oriented businesses differ in where they place initial emphasis when developing offerings. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A product-oriented business first analyses customers' needs and wants before defining product specifications.
A product-oriented business focuses on the product and its specifications first and later thinks about how to sell it.
A market-oriented business will first analyse customers' needs and wants and then tailor products to fulfil these requirements.
Product-oriented and market-oriented businesses may pursue identical marketing objectives even when their strategic starting points differ.
A product-oriented business mainly relies on the quality of the features of the product to be successful in the market.
tactical_explanations:
Product orientation does not begin with a full needs census.

At a business, the firm builds from what it already wants to sell — feature grids, package menus, fixed ladders — and only afterwards looks for buyers who will take that menu. Needs-first, specs-second is market orientation, not product orientation.

So the statement is False.

Product-oriented planning puts the offering and its features ahead of detailed selling plans.

Inside product orientation, a business refines the offering first and develops the sales story around that finished object. Confidence in feature quality carries much of the commercial wager, even though some promotion still happens later.

That distinction is what turns a dry True/False into a teachable board moment.

Students who only memorise the verdict without the contrast usually trip when the industry nouns change.

Name the trap, show the counter-scene, then close — that order keeps the letter honest.

So the statement is True.

Market-oriented workflow listens first, then shapes the product.

At a business, research, loyalty signals, purchase histories, or stated needs lead; the feature list answers that brief. Internal preferences alone do not write the opening specification.

That distinction is what turns a dry True/False into a teachable board moment.

Students who only memorise the verdict without the contrast usually trip when the industry nouns change.

So the statement is True.

Firms may share profitability objectives and still follow different orientation paths.
